title: Weight, mass and the normal force: what pulls a thing down and what holds it up

summary.text: On Jupiter you would weigh about two and a half times as much as on Earth. But you could not stand anywhere to feel it, because Jupiter has no solid ground. Weight is the pull of a world's gravity on a thing, in newtons. Mass is the amount of matter in the thing, in kilograms, and it stays the same on every world. A surface holds a thing up with a normal force, and that force is not always as big as the weight. Your child squashes dough in a pile of books to find where the push is biggest. They also work out weights on other worlds, and draw gravity, normal force and applied force as arrows.
summary.art: A child standing on the tiled floor of a flat with a down arrow and an up arrow of equal length, beside a small picture of the same child falling through the striped clouds of Jupiter with only a down arrow.

intro.hook: Put eight books in a pile on a table. Which book is pushed up the hardest by what lies under it: the top book, a middle book or the bottom book? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: It is hard to tell by looking, because nothing in the pile moves. In the Dough Stack experiment, you put soft dough at three levels of the pile. Then you see which dough is squashed the most. First, in Be the Table, your own hand holds up a book and feels what a table has to do. In this unit you find out what pulls a thing down, what holds it up, and how hard each one acts. You also find out why your weight would change on another world while your mass would not.
intro.art: A pile of eight school notebooks on a table with a question mark beside the top, the middle and the bottom book.

outcomes: By the end I can say how mass and weight are different, and give the unit of each.
By the end I can work out the weight of a thing on the Moon and the planets from its mass.
By the end I can explain why a bigger world does not always pull harder at its surface.
By the end I can say what a normal force is, which way it points, and how a surface makes it.
By the end I can show with a test that a normal force can be bigger or smaller than the weight.
By the end I can name applied forces, and say when an applied force starts and stops.
By the end I can draw a force diagram with gravity, normal force and applied force arrows of the right length.
By the end I can say what scientists still do not know about mass and gravity.

terms.meaning: Mass is the amount of matter in a thing. It is measured in kilograms and grams. The mass of a thing is the same on every world.
terms.example: A 1 kilogram packet of rice has a mass of 1 kilogram in Kochi, on the Moon and on Mars.
terms.art: A packet of rice marked 1 kilogram shown on the Earth, on the Moon and on Mars, with the same label each time.

terms.meaning: Weight is the pull of gravity on a thing. It is a force, so it is measured in newtons. The weight of a thing changes from world to world.
terms.example: A 1 kilogram packet of rice weighs about 10 newtons on Earth and about 1.6 newtons on the Moon.
terms.art: A packet of rice with a long down arrow on Earth and a short down arrow on the Moon.

terms.meaning: A newton is the unit of force. On Earth, gravity pulls 100 grams with a force of about 1 newton.
terms.example: A small apple, or 100 millilitres of water, weighs about 1 newton on Earth.
terms.art: A hand holding a small apple with a short down arrow labelled 1 newton.

terms.meaning: Gravity is the force with which every mass attracts every other mass. The Earth's gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth.
terms.example: A dropped spoon falls towards the centre of the Earth, whether you drop it in Chennai or in Shillong.
terms.art: The Earth with small people standing all round it and an arrow from each pointing to the centre.

terms.meaning: The strength of gravity at a place is the pull on each kilogram there, in newtons for each kilogram. It is about 9.8 on Earth and 1.6 on the Moon.
terms.example: On Mars the strength of gravity is about 3.7 newtons for each kilogram, so a 10 kilogram bag weighs 37 newtons.
terms.art: Three worlds in a row, the Moon, Mars and the Earth, each with a number of newtons per kilogram written under it.

terms.meaning: A non-contact force acts between things that do not touch. Gravity is a non-contact force.
terms.example: The Earth pulls a mango while the mango is still falling through the air.
terms.art: A mango in mid-air below a branch, with a down arrow and nothing touching the mango.

terms.meaning: A contact force acts only while two things touch. The normal force and applied forces are contact forces.
terms.example: The push of your hand on a door stops the moment your hand leaves the door.
terms.art: A hand flat on a door with the touching place circled.

terms.meaning: The normal force is the push of a surface on a thing that presses against it. It points straight out from the surface.
terms.example: A table pushes up on a steel tumbler with a normal force. A wall pushes sideways on a hand that leans on it.
terms.art: A steel tumbler on a table with an arrow pointing straight up from the table into the tumbler.

terms.meaning: Two lines are at right angles when they meet like the corner of a book. In maths, 'normal' means at right angles. That is where the normal force gets its name.
terms.example: On a sloping board, the normal force leans with the board. It still points straight out of the board's surface.
terms.art: A book on a sloping board, with an arrow leaving the board's surface at a square corner.

terms.meaning: An applied force is a push or pull on a thing by someone or something that touches it. A person, an animal or a machine can be the one who pushes or pulls.
terms.example: A bullock pulling a cart, a hand pressing a rolling pin and a crane lifting a beam all apply forces.
terms.art: A hand pressing down on a rolling pin over a round of dough, with an arrow from the hand.

terms.meaning: A force diagram is a simple drawing of one thing, with an arrow for each force on it. Each arrow points the way the force acts. A bigger force gets a longer arrow.
terms.example: A book on a table gets two arrows of equal length. Gravity points down and the normal force points up.
terms.art: A box drawn as a rectangle with a down arrow labelled gravity and an up arrow labelled normal force.

terms.meaning: Forces on a thing are balanced when they cancel each other. A thing that stays still has balanced forces on it.
terms.example: A bucket standing on the floor is still. The floor's push up is as big as the pull of gravity down.
terms.art: A bucket on a floor with an up arrow and a down arrow of the same length.

terms.meaning: A load is the weight that a surface or a support has to hold up.
terms.example: The bottom book in a pile of eight carries a load of seven books.
terms.art: A pile of eight books with a bracket round the top seven, labelled load on the bottom book.

terms.meaning: To compress a thing is to squash it, so that its parts are pushed closer together. A compressed thing pushes back.
terms.example: A sofa cushion is compressed when you sit on it, and it pushes up on you.
terms.art: A cushion squashed under a sitting child, with small arrows inside the cushion pointing up.

terms.meaning: Inertia is how hard it is to change the movement of a thing. More mass means more inertia. Inertia does not depend on gravity.
terms.example: A full water can is harder to start swinging than an empty one, and harder to stop.
terms.art: Two bottles hanging on strings, one full and one nearly empty, with a finger pushing each.

terms.meaning: A gas giant is a very large planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It has no solid surface to stand on. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.
terms.example: A spacecraft that drops into Jupiter keeps sinking through thicker and thicker gas.
terms.art: A small probe on a parachute sinking through layers of orange and white cloud that get darker lower down.

explanations.definition: Mass is the amount of matter in a thing, in kilograms. Weight is the pull of gravity on that thing, in newtons.
explanations.description: People often use the two words for the same thing, and shops call the mass printed on a packet its 'net weight'. In science they are two different quantities. Mass belongs to the thing. A packet of rice has the same grains, and so the same mass, wherever you take it. Weight is a force between the thing and a world. It depends on how strongly that world pulls. To find a weight, multiply the mass by the strength of gravity. On Earth that strength is about 9.8 newtons for each kilogram, and for quick sums we use 10. So 1 kilogram weighs about 10 newtons, and 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. Mass also shows up in a second way. A thing with more mass is harder to start moving and harder to stop. This is called inertia, and it is the same on every world.
examples: A 3 kilogram school bag weighs about 30 newtons on Earth. On the Moon its mass is still 3 kilograms, and it weighs about 5 newtons.
In Hit the Bottles, a string held up each bottle's weight. The full bottle was still much harder to hit away than the nearly empty one.
An Apollo astronaut with suit and backpack had a mass of more than 150 kilograms. On the Moon he felt light, but he was still slow to start, stop and turn.
explanations.art: A school bag on a two-pan balance reading 3 kilograms on Earth and on the Moon, and the same bag on a spring scale showing a long stretch on Earth and a short stretch on the Moon.

explanations.concept: Gravity pulls towards the centre of the Earth
explanations.definition: Gravity is a non-contact force. The Earth's gravity pulls every thing towards the centre of the Earth, whether the thing is still or moving.
explanations.description: Gravity needs no touching. It pulls a book on a table, a book in your hand and a book in mid-air equally hard. Nothing can switch it off, and no wall or roof blocks it. 'Down' means towards the centre of the Earth. So down in Chennai and down in Peru, on the other side of the Earth, point in nearly opposite ways. In a force diagram, the gravity arrow starts at the middle of the thing and points straight down. Gravity pulls both ways. The Earth pulls you, and you pull the Earth just as hard. The Earth has so much mass that your pull does not move it in any way we can measure.
examples: A plumb line, a stone on a thread, hangs along the line that points to the centre of the Earth. Masons use one to build a wall straight up.
A ball thrown upward slows down, stops and comes back. Gravity pulled it down all the way up and all the way down.
The Moon is 384,000 kilometres away, and the Earth's gravity still pulls it. That pull keeps the Moon in its orbit.
explanations.art: The Earth cut away to show its centre, with people standing in India and in Peru and an arrow from each pointing to the centre.

explanations.concept: Weight on the Moon and the planets
explanations.definition: A thing's weight on any world is its mass multiplied by the strength of gravity there, in newtons for each kilogram.
explanations.description: The strength of gravity, in newtons for each kilogram, is about 1.6 on the Moon. It is 3.7 on Mercury and on Mars, and 8.9 on Venus and on Uranus. It is 9.8 on Earth, 10.4 on Saturn, 11.2 on Neptune and about 25 on Jupiter. For the four giant planets, the number is measured at the cloud tops, because they have no ground. So a child with a mass of 30 kilograms weighs about 300 newtons on Earth. The same child weighs 48 newtons on the Moon, 111 on Mars and 750 on Jupiter. The child has not changed at all. On the Moon the child could jump about six times as high. A thrown ball would also fly about six times as far. Catching that ball would feel the same as on Earth, because its mass is the same.
examples: Pragyan, the rover that Chandrayaan-3 carried to the Moon in 2023, has a mass of about 26 kilograms. It weighs about 260 newtons on Earth and about 42 newtons on the Moon.
A 1 litre bottle of water weighs about 10 newtons on Earth, 3.7 newtons on Mars and 25 newtons on Jupiter.
A two-pan balance gives the same answer on every world, because it compares two masses. A spring scale does not, because it measures a pull.
explanations.art: A row of worlds from the Moon to Jupiter, each with the same child and a down arrow whose length matches the child's weight there.

explanations.concept: A bigger world does not always pull harder
explanations.definition: The strength of gravity at the surface of a world depends on two things: the mass of the world, and how far the surface is from its centre.
explanations.description: More mass makes the pull stronger. More distance from the centre makes it weaker. At twice the distance, the pull is one quarter as strong. At three times the distance, it is one ninth. In the Spreading Square, the light from a small torch covered 4 times the area at twice the distance. The pull of a world spreads out round it in the same way. This is a model of how the pull spreads out, and Newton showed in 1687 that gravity follows it. To compare a world with the Earth, take its mass and divide it by its width multiplied by itself. Measure the mass and the width in Earths, so that the Earth counts as 1 for each. Saturn has 95 times the mass of the Earth, so you might expect a crushing pull. But Saturn is also about 9.5 times as wide, so its cloud tops are very far from its centre. 9.5 times 9.5 is about 90, and 95 divided by 90 is just over 1. So the pull at Saturn's cloud tops is only a little stronger than on Earth. Uranus has 14.5 times the Earth's mass and is 4 times as wide. 14.5 divided by 16 is about 0.9, so Uranus pulls a little less than the Earth.
examples: In the Spreading Square, the lit square at 90 centimetres had 9 times the area of the one at 30. At 3 times the distance, each part got one ninth of the light.
Jupiter has 318 times the Earth's mass and is about 11.2 times as wide. 318 divided by 125 is about 2.5, so its pull is about two and a half times the Earth's.
Mercury and Mars both have a strength of gravity of 3.7. Mars is bigger and has more mass, but its surface is further from its centre.
On a high mountain you are a little further from the Earth's centre. So you weigh very slightly less than at the seashore.
explanations.art: Saturn and the Earth drawn side by side to scale, with a long line from Saturn's centre to its cloud tops and a short line from the Earth's centre to its surface.

explanations.concept: The normal force: the push of a surface
explanations.definition: The normal force is the push of a surface on a thing that presses against it. It is a contact force, and it points straight out from the surface, at right angles to it.
explanations.description: A book on a table does not fall, though gravity pulls it all the time. So something must push it up. That push is the normal force from the table. Every surface can give one: a floor, a chair, a palm, a wall, the ground. The word 'normal' here is a maths word that means at right angles. It comes from 'norma', the Latin name for a carpenter's square. On a level table the normal force points straight up. On a sloping board it leans with the board. A wall gives a normal force that points sideways, into your hand when you lean on it. A surface can only push. It cannot pull a thing towards itself.
examples: You sit on a chair. The seat pushes up on you, and the floor pushes up on your feet. Both are normal forces.
A ladder leans on a wall. The wall pushes the top of the ladder sideways, straight out from the wall.
A ball in mid-air touches no surface, so no normal force acts on it. Only gravity and the air act on the ball.
explanations.art: Three small drawings with a normal force arrow in each: a book on a level table, a book on a sloping board and a hand leaning on a wall.

explanations.concept: How a surface pushes back by the right amount
explanations.definition: A surface is compressed or bent by a load, and that makes it push back. It gives way until its push is as big as the force pressing on it.
explanations.description: Sit on a rope cot and the ropes dip. Stretched ropes pull back, like the rubber band in a catapult. The more they dip, the harder they push you up. They stop dipping when their push equals your weight. A heavier person makes them dip further. A cushion, a mattress and a sponge do the same, and you can see it. A table and a stone floor do it too, but they give way far too little for you to see. Underneath, every solid is made of atoms that hold each other at a set distance. Press them closer and they push back with electric forces, the way a compressed spring does. So no surface has to be told how heavy a thing is. The thing sinks in until the forces balance. If the load is too big for the material, the surface breaks.
examples: In the Dough Stack, the dough under more books was squashed wider. More load pressed it further before it stopped.
A bathroom scale has a stiff metal part inside that bends very slightly when you stand on it. The scale measures that bending.
A thin shelf sags under a row of heavy books. A thick shelf sags too, by an amount too small to see.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in view of a table top under a tumbler, with rows of atoms drawn as balls joined by small springs, pressed slightly closer together under the tumbler.

explanations.concept: The normal force is not always as big as the weight
explanations.definition: A normal force is as big as it needs to be to stop a thing sinking into the surface. That can be more than the thing's weight, less than it, or nothing.
explanations.description: For one book lying alone on a level table, the normal force equals the book's weight. Many books stop there, but it is only the simplest case. Press down on the book with your hand, and the table must push up against the weight and your push together. Lift the book a little with a string, and the table has less to do. Put the book at the bottom of a pile, and the table pushes it up with the weight of the whole pile. Put the book on a slope, and the normal force is smaller than the weight. The slope only stops the book sinking into it. Friction stops the book sliding down. When you jump, you push down hard on the floor, and the floor pushes you up with more than your weight. A runner's foot gets a push from the ground of two to three times the runner's weight at each step.
examples: In the Dough Stack, the table pushed up on the bottom book with the weight of all eight books.
In Lift, Press and Tilt, a packet on a kitchen scale read less when a string lifted it. It read more when a finger pressed it down.
In Lift, Press and Tilt, the packet read less and less as the board under the scale was tilted more steeply.
You hang from a bar with your feet off the floor. The floor's normal force on you is zero.
explanations.art: Four drawings of the same book: alone on a table, pressed by a hand, at the bottom of a pile and on a slope, each with a normal force arrow of a different length.

explanations.definition: An applied force is a push or a pull that a person, another animal or a machine puts on a thing. It is a contact force.
explanations.description: You apply a force when you lift a bag or press a rolling pin. You also do it when you pull a drawer, kick a ball or push a swing. A bullock applies a force to a cart, and a crane applies one to a beam. An applied force can point any way: up, down or sideways. It starts when the touching starts and stops when the touching stops. A ball that has left your hand has no force from the hand on it any more. It keeps moving because a moving thing goes on moving unless some force slows it or turns it. Gravity then curves its path down, and the air slows it. Applied forces also change normal forces. Press down on a table and the floor under the table legs pushes up harder. Lift one end of a bench and the floor under that end pushes less.
examples: A person pressing dosa batter out of a ladle, a potter pressing clay and a tailor pulling thread all apply forces.
In Be the Table, a grown-up pressed down on the books, and your palm had to push up harder.
A cricket ball flying to the boundary has two forces on it: gravity and air resistance. The bat's push ended when the ball left the bat.
explanations.art: A child pushing a younger child on a swing, with an arrow from the pushing hands, and the same swing a moment later with no hand and no arrow.

explanations.definition: A force diagram shows one thing and every force on it as an arrow. If the thing stays still, the forces on it are balanced.
explanations.description: Draw the thing as a simple box. Draw one arrow for each force, starting from the box and pointing the way the force acts. Make a bigger force a longer arrow, and label each arrow. Only forces on the thing go in the diagram, never the forces it puts on other things. Then check the balance. For a thing that stays still, the up arrows together must be as long as the down arrows together. A 1 kilogram packet on a table has gravity of 10 newtons down and a normal force of 10 newtons up. If a string pulls the packet up with 3 newtons, the normal force shrinks to 7 newtons. 7 and 3 up still balance 10 down. If the forces do not balance, the thing speeds up, slows down or turns.
examples: A bag held still in your hand: gravity points down, and the applied force from your hand points up, with the same length.
The bottom book of a pile: gravity and the push of the books above point down. One long normal force arrow points up.
A ball at the top of a throw has only one arrow, which is gravity pointing down. So the ball cannot stay there, and it starts to fall.
explanations.art: A notebook page with three neat force diagrams: a packet on a table, a packet lifted partly by a string and a bag held in a hand.

explanations.concept: Loads are passed down, all the way into the Earth
explanations.definition: Each surface in a pile holds up everything above it. So the load grows towards the bottom, and in the end the Earth holds it.
explanations.description: The top book of a pile presses on the second. The second presses on the third with its own weight and the top book's weight. So the load is passed down and grows at each level. The table carries the whole pile and passes that load through its legs to the floor. The floor passes it to the walls and pillars, and they pass it to the ground. The same thing happens inside the Earth. Rock deep down carries all the rock above it. At the centre of the Earth the squeeze is about 3.6 million times the push of the air around you. This sets a limit on mountains. A mountain that is too tall crushes the rock at its own base. On Mars a rock weighs much less, and that is one reason Mars has taller mountains. Its volcano Olympus Mons is about 22 kilometres high, two and a half times the height of Mount Everest. Weight also makes big worlds round. In a world wider than several hundred kilometres, the load is big enough to crush any tall lump down.
examples: In the Dough Stack, the dough under eight books was squashed wider than the dough under one book.
In the Load on the Pillar, a ground-floor pillar held up six floors. It carried about six times the load of a pillar under the roof.
Small asteroids are lumpy, like potatoes. Their weight is too small to crush rock into a ball.
explanations.art: A cutaway drawing of a pile of books on a table in a flat, with arrows that grow longer level by level, down through the table legs, the floor, the pillars and into the ground.

explanations.concept: Worlds with nothing to stand on
explanations.definition: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, and Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. None of them has a solid surface, so nothing there gives a normal force to stand on.
explanations.description: Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium. What we see in photographs is the top of its clouds. Below the clouds the gas gets thicker, hotter and more squeezed. Deep down the hydrogen is pressed into a liquid. A person there would have weight, because Jupiter's gravity would pull hard. But nothing would push back, so the person would keep sinking. A scale works by measuring the push between you and a surface. On Jupiter there is no surface to push back, so a scale would have nothing to measure. That is why we give a giant planet's strength of gravity at its cloud tops. The Sun has no surface either. Its strength of gravity at the top of its glowing gas is about 274 newtons for each kilogram.
examples: In 1995 the Galileo probe dropped into Jupiter on a parachute. It sank for about an hour and never met a surface.
Saturn has less mass in each litre than water has. A piece of Saturn would float in a big enough sea.
A person floating in a pool has weight, but the pool floor gives no normal force. The water holds the person up with upthrust.
explanations.art: A person-sized figure with a long down arrow and no up arrow, sinking through layers of Jupiter's clouds.

explanations.concept: Why does mass do two jobs?
explanations.definition: Mass sets how hard gravity pulls a thing. Mass also sets how hard the thing is to speed up. Scientists have ideas about why the two always match, but no agreed answer.
explanations.description: The two jobs could have been set by two different amounts. A stone might have had a lot of 'gravity mass' and only a little inertia. But every test finds that the two are equal. That is why a heavy and a light thing fall together when no air is in the way. Isaac Newton checked it in the 1680s with two pendulums. He filled their boxes with gold, lead, glass, sand, salt, wood, water and wheat. All of them swung in step, to within one part in a thousand. In 2022 a French satellite called MICROSCOPE reported a far finer test. Two metal cylinders fell around the Earth together, and they matched each other to about one part in a thousand million million.
examples: A full bottle is pulled ten times as hard as a bottle that is one tenth full. It is also ten times as hard to speed up. The two effects cancel out, so both bottles fall together.
On the Moon in 1971, the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon's feather. They landed together.

perspectives.explanation: The two kinds of mass are found to be equal by experiment. Newton gave no reason for it.
Gravity is not a pull on each thing. Mass bends space and time, and every falling thing follows the same bent path. So all things must fall alike.
Einstein's idea fits every test so far. But it has not been joined with the physics of the very small. So the match may yet fail at some very fine level.

explanations.art: Two pendulums of the same length swinging side by side, one with a box of gold and one with a box of wheat.

agreed.text: Mass stays the same on every world, and weight changes with the strength of gravity.
agreed.evidence: Moon rocks that astronauts carried home weigh about six times as much on Earth as they did on the Moon. Their mass is unchanged.

agreed.text: The Earth's gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Plumb lines hang towards the centre at every place on Earth, and people stand upright all round the globe.

agreed.text: A surface pushes back on anything that presses on it, with a force at right angles to the surface.
agreed.evidence: Scales and force sensors measure this push directly. Engineers use it to design every floor, bridge and chair.

agreed.text: Solid surfaces give way a little under every load, even when we cannot see it.
agreed.evidence: Fine instruments measure the tiny bending of floors, bridges and steel beams. A digital scale works by measuring such bending.

agreed.text: A thing that stays still has balanced forces on it.
agreed.evidence: This follows from Newton's laws of motion, published in 1687. Every building that stands is a test of it.

agreed.text: Jupiter and Saturn have no solid surface.
agreed.evidence: Their average density is far too low for solid rock. In 1995 the Galileo probe sank into Jupiter for about an hour and met only gas.

challenging.claim: The normal force on a thing is always equal to its weight.
challenging.for: It is true for one thing resting alone on a level surface, which is the picture most books draw.
challenging.against: In the Dough Stack, the table pushed the bottom book up with the weight of eight books. On a slope the normal force is smaller than the weight. In a jump it is bigger.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule in many books: that the normal force always equals the weight.

challenging.claim: A table cannot push, because it is not alive and has no muscles.
challenging.for: A table does not move or get tired, and we cannot see it doing anything.
challenging.against: A book on a table stays still though gravity pulls it. So an upward force must act on the book. Soft surfaces show the cause: they are compressed and push back. Hard surfaces are compressed too, by an amount too small to see.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a table, a floor or a wall can really push.

challenging.claim: A thrown ball carries the force of the throw along with it.
challenging.who: John Philoponus in the 500s and Jean Buridan in the 1300s, and most people's first idea
challenging.for: The ball keeps moving after it leaves the hand, so it seems that something from the hand must still be pushing it.
challenging.against: An applied force is a contact force, so it ends when the hand lets go. A moving thing keeps moving with no push at all. Gravity and the air are the only forces on the ball in flight.
challenging.context: This card is about what pushes a ball after it has left the hand.

challenging.claim: A planet with more mass always has stronger gravity at its surface.
challenging.for: More mass does make a stronger pull, and Jupiter, the planet with the most mass, has the strongest pull.
challenging.against: The distance from the centre matters too. Saturn has 95 times the Earth's mass. But its cloud tops are so far from its centre that the pull there is about the same as on Earth. Uranus pulls less than the Earth.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a bigger planet always pulls harder at its surface.

challenging.claim: 'Weight' should mean what a scale shows, and not the pull of gravity.
challenging.who: Some physics teachers and textbook writers
challenging.for: A scale is how we measure weight in real life. With this meaning, an astronaut in orbit really is weightless, which matches what the astronaut feels.
challenging.against: Most textbooks keep 'weight' for the pull of gravity, which is nearly as strong in orbit as on the ground. They use 'normal force' or 'apparent weight' for what the scale shows.
challenging.context: This card is about what the word 'weight' should mean. Scientists agree on the facts and argue about the word.

challenging.claim: Gravity is not really a force.
challenging.who: Albert Einstein, in his general theory of relativity of 1915
challenging.for: Einstein's theory says that mass bends space and time, and that falling things simply follow the bend. It predicts the bending of starlight and the timing of satellite clocks correctly.
challenging.against: For everything in this unit, treating gravity as a force gives the right answers. Engineers and space agencies still use Newton's force for almost all their sums.
challenging.context: This card is about a deeper view of gravity. In it, the Earth does not pull a thing at all.

big_questions.q: The Earth pulls a book down, and the Earth, through the table and the floor, holds the book up. Is the Earth doing one thing or two?
big_questions.hint: Follow the load down from the book, level by level. Where does it end?

big_questions.q: Your weight changes from world to world, and your mass does not. Which of the two tells more about you?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would still have with no world near you at all.

big_questions.q: A table pushes up on a book by exactly the right amount. Does the table have to know the book's weight?
big_questions.hint: Think about how the dough stopped spreading under the books.

big_questions.q: In every pile, the bottom carries the most. Where in a family, a school or a city is there a 'bottom book'?
big_questions.hint: Think about whose work everything else rests on, and whether people notice it.

big_questions.q: On Jupiter you would have weight and nothing to stand on. Can a thing be heavy if nothing ever holds it up?
big_questions.hint: Is 'heavy' about the pull, or about what you feel when a surface pushes back?

big_questions.q: Mountains on Mars can be taller than mountains on Earth. What else about a world might its gravity decide?
big_questions.hint: Think about the heights of trees, the legs of animals and the shapes of buildings.

big_questions.q: Shops sell rice by the kilogram, which is mass, but they measure it with a pull. Is that fair on every floor of every building?
big_questions.hint: A balance compares masses. A spring scale measures weight. Which would you trust on a mountain?

story.title: The Slow Start
story.note: A made-up story. Revathi Chithi, Thenu, Karthik and the cable test are imagined. These things are real. The rover Pragyan has six wheels, a mass of about 26 kilograms, and travelled on the Moon at about 1 centimetre each second. It was carried by Chandrayaan-3, which landed on 23 August 2023. ISRO tested its Moon rovers on a copy of Moon soil made from rock from Tamil Nadu. Space agencies do use cables, counterweights or balloons to make a machine feel as light on Earth as it would on the Moon. The Moon's strength of gravity is about 1.6 newtons for each kilogram, about one sixth of the Earth's.
text: Thenu was ten, and it was her first time inside the satellite centre in Bengaluru. It was Family Day. Her aunt Revathi worked here, and she had promised to show Thenu the rover.

The test hall was as big as a school ground. Half of the floor was a long grey tray, filled with rock powder. "It comes from hills in Tamil Nadu," said Revathi Chithi. "We ground it very fine, so that it behaves like the soil on the Moon."

At the edge of the tray stood a small machine on six wheels, about the size of a big suitcase. Thenu bent down to look at it. "This is Pragyan," said Chithi. "Twenty-six kilograms. It is going to the Moon on Chandrayaan-3."

A young engineer called Karthik was kneeling beside it with a laptop. He had joined the team two months ago. "On the Moon it will weigh six times less," he told Thenu happily. "Twenty-six kilograms will feel like four, as light as a school bag. It will run even better there than here. Watch."
He pressed a key. The six wheels began to turn, and the rover rolled out across the grey powder, with a neat line of tracks behind it. "See?" said Karthik.
Thenu frowned. "But here it is six times heavier than on the Moon," she said. "So how do you know it will run the same way there?"
Karthik opened his mouth, and shut it again.

"That is the right question," said Chithi. "We cannot take the Moon to Bengaluru. So we take the weight away." She pointed up. A strong cable hung from a crane in the roof, with a counterweight on its other end. "This cable will hold up five sixths of the rover's weight. The ground will carry only one sixth, as it will on the Moon."

They rolled the rover onto a flat parcel scale in the floor, and Thenu read it. "Twenty-six kilograms." Then they clipped on the cable and lifted a little. Thenu read the scale again. "Four kilograms," she said.

"The scale shows how hard the ground pushes up," said Chithi. "With the cable helping, the ground pushes only a sixth as hard. A wheel grips by pressing on the ground. A sixth of the press gives a sixth of the grip."

Karthik gave the wheels the same full power as before. This time they spun at once. The powder flew up behind them in grey sprays, and a small hill of dust grew behind each wheel. The rover hardly moved.
"Stop," said Chithi. Karthik stopped it. He looked puzzled. "I thought less weight would make everything easier. It must be the motors. I will turn up the power."
"That will make it worse," said Chithi.

"Easier for some things," she went on. "It is easier to lift. But look at this." She put her hand against the rover, with the cable holding it up, and pushed. It moved slowly. She pushed harder, and it moved a little faster. "Thenu, you try."
Thenu pushed. The rover felt solid and slow, like a full steel almirah on a smooth floor. "It is heavy," she said. "But you said it only weighs four kilograms now."

"Its weight is only a sixth. Its mass is the same," said Chithi. "Mass is how much of it there is, and that is the same on every world. Mass is what makes it hard to start moving. So the motors must still start twenty-six kilograms of rover. But the wheels have only a sixth of the grip to push with."
Karthik sat back on his heels. "So the push from the motors is as big as before, and the grip is smaller. That is why the wheels spin."
"Then what do we change?" asked Thenu.
"We cannot change the Moon," said Chithi, smiling. "We change the start. A wheel will hold, if the push grows slowly enough."

Karthik typed a new line. The motors began to turn very gently, and the push grew a little more every second. The six wheels bit into the powder. The rover rolled forward, slowly, and left a neat line of tracks behind it.
"There," said Chithi. "Slow is the speed at which a wheel holds."

Months later, Thenu sat in front of the television at home on the evening of the landing. Karthik had sent her a message. The lander stood on the Moon, and a ramp came down. Then Pragyan rolled out onto the grey soil.
"It is so slow," said her little brother.
"About one centimetre each second," said Thenu. "That is how fast its wheels can hold the ground."
story.epiphany: For the parent: on the Moon the rover has the same mass but only about one sixth of the weight. So the ground pushes up on its wheels one sixth as hard, and the wheels grip less. The motors still have to move all 26 kilograms of mass, because mass is what makes a thing hard to start moving. Grip is lower and the mass is the same, so a hard start makes the wheels spin. A slow start keeps the wheels holding. A thing that is lighter is not always easier to move.
ask: The ground pushed up on each wheel less in the cable test. Why did the wheels grip less?
The rover weighs six times less on the Moon. Does its mass change too?
Why did a harder push from the motors make the wheels spin more?
How did a slow start help the wheels grip?
Where have you seen a wheel or a foot slip when someone starts too fast?

games.title: Bigger, The Same, Smaller or Zero? The surface-push card game
games.context: This is a card game about the normal force. Each card describes a thing with a surface or support under it. You show with a sign card whether the push is bigger than the weight, the same, smaller or zero.

printables.title: 20 situation cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A steel tumbler stands still on a kitchen shelf. How hard does the shelf push up on it, compared with the tumbler's weight?
items.b: THE SAME. The tumbler stays still, so the shelf's push balances its weight.

items.f: A rice packet lies on a table. You press down on it with a finger. How hard does the table push up, compared with the packet's weight?
items.b: BIGGER. The table must push against the weight and the finger's press together.

items.f: A packet on a kitchen scale is partly lifted by a string in your hand. How hard does the scale push up, compared with the packet's weight?
items.b: SMALLER. The string carries part of the weight, so the scale carries less.

items.f: You hang from a bar with both feet off the floor. How hard does the floor push up on you?
items.b: ZERO. Your feet do not touch the floor, so it cannot push. Your hands pull on the bar instead.

items.f: A book rests on a board tilted at 30 degrees and does not slide. How hard does the board push on the book, compared with the book's weight?
items.b: SMALLER. On a slope, the board's push is less than the weight. Friction holds the rest along the slope.

items.f: You crouch and then push off the floor with both feet to jump. While your feet push, how hard does the floor push up on you, compared with your weight?
items.b: BIGGER. You push down hard on the floor, so it pushes up with more than your weight. That is how you speed up.

items.f: Five equal books lie in a pile. How hard does the table push up on the whole pile, compared with the weight of one book?
items.b: BIGGER. The table holds all five books, so its push is 5 times the weight of one book.

items.f: A ball is thrown up and is at the top of its flight. How hard does a surface push on it?
items.b: ZERO. The ball touches nothing. Only gravity pulls on it, so it starts to fall.

items.f: A girl stands still on a bathroom scale. How hard does the scale push up on her, compared with her weight?
items.b: THE SAME. She stays still, so the scale's push balances her weight. That push is what the scale shows.

items.f: A lift starts to go up. How hard does the floor push up on you, compared with your weight?
items.b: BIGGER. The floor must push harder to make you speed up, so you feel heavier for a moment.

items.f: A lift starts to go down. How hard does the floor push up on you, compared with your weight?
items.b: SMALLER. The floor pushes less while you speed up downwards, so you feel lighter for a moment.

items.f: A box stands on the floor, 1 metre from a wall. Nobody touches the box. How hard does the wall push on the box?
items.b: ZERO. A wall pushes only on things that press against it.

items.f: A car is parked on a level road. How hard do its four tyres together push up on the car, compared with the car's weight?
items.b: THE SAME. The car stays still, so the road's push balances the car's weight.

items.f: A book lies on a table on the Moon. How hard does the table push up on it, compared with the book's weight there?
items.b: THE SAME. The book weighs less on the Moon, and the table pushes less by the same amount.

items.f: A girl floats still in a swimming pool, with her toes not touching the floor. How hard does the pool floor push on her?
items.b: ZERO. Water holds her up with upthrust. The floor does not touch her.

items.f: A runner's foot hits the ground at each step. How hard does the ground push up on the foot, compared with the runner's weight?
items.b: BIGGER. At each step the push is about 2 to 3 times the runner's weight.

items.f: A book lies on a table. A second equal book is put on top of it. How hard does the table push up on the bottom book, compared with that book's weight?
items.b: BIGGER. The table holds up both books, so its push is twice the bottom book's weight.

items.f: A packet lies on a table. A string pulls it up with half of the packet's weight. How hard does the table push up on the packet, compared with its weight?
items.b: SMALLER. The string carries half, so the table carries the other half.

items.f: A cat sits still on a table. How hard does the table push up on her, compared with her weight?
items.b: THE SAME. She stays still, so the table's push balances her weight.

items.f: An astronaut floats inside the space station. How hard does a wall push on her?
items.b: ZERO. She and the station fall together, so nothing presses her against the wall.

printables.title: 4 sign cards for each player: BIGGER, THE SAME, SMALLER, ZERO

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up. Each player takes a set of 4 sign cards.
One player reads the top card aloud. Everyone thinks for 10 seconds.
On the count of three, every player holds up one sign card.
Turn the card over and read the answer and the reason. A player scores 1 point for the right sign, and 1 more for giving the reason in their own words.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: score 1 point for each right sign. Try to reach 16 out of 20, then play again.

setup.art: Twenty cut-out cards in a pile on a table, with four sign cards in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the sign cards. Make a pile.

setup.art: A reader holding a card and two players each holding up a sign card that says BIGGER or THE SAME.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone holds up a sign.

setup.art: The card turned over to show the answer, with a score sheet beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Read the answer. Score the points.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Cut out 4 sign cards for each player. 3. Shuffle the cards. 4. Put them in a pile, question side up.
flow.say: Each card shows a thing with something pushing up on it. We decide whether the push is bigger than the weight, the same, smaller or zero. Sometimes the answer will surprise us.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the signs. Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bigger, The Same, Smaller or Zero. Here you set up the cards and the sign cards.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone holds up a sign. 4. Turn the card over and read the reason. 5. Score the points.
flow.say: Ask yourself two questions. Is the surface touching the thing? And is anything else pushing or pulling the thing up or down?
flow.kid: Read the card. Is it touching? Is anything else pushing or pulling? Hold up your sign.

ask.q: A lift starts to go up. Why is the floor's push bigger than your weight?
good: The floor must push harder to make you speed up.
You feel heavier for a moment.

flow.parent: If the surface does not touch the thing, the push is zero. If something else pushes the thing down, the surface pushes harder. If something else pulls it up, the surface pushes less. If nothing else acts and the thing is still, the push is the same as the weight.
flow.context: This is the main part of Bigger, The Same, Smaller or Zero. Here you read each card and hold up a sign.

flow.do: 1. Count your points. 2. Lay out the cards anyone got wrong. 3. Sort all 20 cards into four heaps: bigger, the same, smaller and zero. 4. Look at each heap and find what the cards in it have in common.
flow.say: Which cards surprised us? Sort the cards into four heaps. What do the cards in each heap have in common?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into four heaps. What do the heaps have in common?
flow.parent: The cards in the bigger heap all have an extra push down or a speeding up. The smaller heap has a pull up or a slope. The zero heap has no touching. The same heap has a thing still on a level surface.

check.q: A girl stands still on a bathroom scale. How does the scale's push compare with her weight?
check.why: She stays still, and nothing else pushes or pulls her up or down. So the scale's push balances her weight. That push is what the scale shows. Choosing bigger or smaller means thinking that something else is acting on her.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bigger, The Same, Smaller or Zero. Here you count the points and sort the cards.

games.title: World Ladder: which world makes you heaviest?
games.context: This is a card game about the strength of gravity on different worlds. Each round you draw three world cards and put the worlds in order, heaviest first.

printables.title: 11 world cards to cut out (the strength of gravity is on the back)

items.f: Pluto
items.b: 0.6 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 18 newtons.

items.f: Titan, a moon of Saturn
items.b: 1.4 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 42 newtons.

items.f: The Moon
items.b: 1.6 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 48 newtons.

items.f: Io, a moon of Jupiter
items.b: 1.8 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 54 newtons.

items.f: Mars
items.b: 3.7 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 111 newtons.

items.f: Venus
items.b: 8.9 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 267 newtons.

items.f: The Earth
items.b: 9.8 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 290 newtons.

items.f: Saturn, at the cloud tops (a star: no solid ground)
items.b: 10.4 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 312 newtons.

items.f: Neptune, at the cloud tops (a star: no solid ground)
items.b: 11.2 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 336 newtons.

items.f: Jupiter, at the cloud tops (a star: no solid ground)
items.b: About 25 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 750 newtons.

items.f: The Sun, at the top of its glowing gas (a star: no solid ground)
items.b: 274 newtons for each kilogram. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms would weigh about 8,220 newtons.

rules: Shuffle the world cards and put them in a pile, name side up.
In each round, the reader turns over 3 cards and reads the names. Each player writes the three worlds in order, from the one that makes you heaviest to the lightest.
Turn the cards over. Everyone checks their order against the numbers.
Score 3 points for the whole order right, or 1 point for just the heaviest. Score 1 bonus point for naming each world with no solid ground, as shown by the star on the card.
Shuffle all the cards again after every 3 rounds. Play 6 rounds. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: score the same way, and try to reach 12 points in 6 rounds.

setup.art: Eleven world cards in a pile, with a pencil and paper beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the world cards. Make a pile.

setup.art: Three cards turned up, Mars, Saturn and the Moon, with a player writing the three names in order.
setup.caption: 2. Turn up three cards. Write them in order, heaviest first.

setup.art: The three cards turned over to show the numbers, and a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cards over. Check your order and score the points.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 11 world cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile with the names facing up. 4. Fetch a pencil and paper for each player.
flow.say: Each card is a world. We will guess where each one belongs on the ladder of gravity. The numbers on the back will tell us who is right.
flow.kid: Cut out the world cards. Shuffle them. Put them in a pile, name side up.
flow.context: This is the first step of World Ladder. Here you set up the cards.

flow.do: 1. Turn up 3 cards. 2. Everyone writes the three worlds in order, heaviest first. 3. Turn the cards over and read the numbers. 4. Score the points. 5. Play 6 rounds.
flow.say: Which world will make you heaviest? Remember the pull depends on the mass of the world and also on its width. A bigger world does not always pull harder.
flow.kid: Turn up 3 cards. Write them in order, heaviest first. Check the numbers.

ask.q: Saturn has 95 times the Earth's mass. Why does it make you only a little heavier than the Earth does?
good: Its cloud tops are very far from its centre, so the pull there is only a little more.
The width counts twice.

ask.q: Why does Jupiter give such a large number?
good: It has 318 times the Earth's mass, and only 11 times the width.

flow.parent: If your child puts Saturn above Neptune, ask why. Saturn has more mass than Neptune but is wider, so Neptune's pull at the cloud tops is a little bigger. The numbers on the cards decide, not the sizes of the worlds.
flow.context: This is the main part of World Ladder. Here you order the worlds and check the numbers.

flow.do: 1. Count your points. 2. Put all 11 cards in order on the table, from the weakest gravity to the strongest. 3. Find the starred cards. 4. Ask which world on the ladder you could really stand on.
flow.say: Put all eleven cards in one ladder. Where is the Earth on it? Which worlds could you really stand on? Which have no ground?
flow.kid: Put all the cards in one ladder. Where is Earth? Which have no ground?
flow.parent: The Earth sits near the middle. Many worlds pull less than the Earth. Only Jupiter and the Sun pull far more than the Earth does. The starred worlds have no solid ground to stand on.

check.q: Which of these three worlds gives the biggest weight?
check.why: Jupiter's number is about 25, much more than Saturn's 10.4 or the Moon's 1.6. Choosing Saturn mixes up the size of the world with the pull at its top. The Sun has a bigger number still, 274.

flow.context: This is the last step of World Ladder. Here you build the whole ladder and think about standing on it.

experiments.title: The Dough Stack: which level of a pile is pushed up the hardest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a pile of eight books with a ball of soft dough at three levels. The dough shows how hard the books above it press down. You measure how wide each ball is squashed.
experiments.question: In a pile of eight books, which level is pushed up the hardest by what lies under it: the top, the middle or the bottom? And what happens to the bottom dough if someone presses down on the pile?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which of the three balls of dough will be squashed the widest? Then guess what a hand pressing on the pile will do to the bottom ball. Write both guesses and your reason for each. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use balls of dough that are the same size, from the same dough. Put each ball at the same spot on its book. Keep the books on the dough for the same 5 minutes each time. Measure the widest part of each ball with the same ruler. Do the whole test twice with new dough, because one run can be a fluke.

materials.item: eight books or thick notebooks of about the same size, each between 250 and 400 grams
a cup of atta and a little water, for stiff dough
a plain sheet of paper, cut into 6 squares of about 4 centimetres
a 30 centimetre ruler with millimetre marks
a kitchen scale in grams, to check one book (it is not needed if the books are about the same)
a plate to knead the dough on, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Build the pile on a flat table, away from the edge. Keep your feet out from under it. Wash your hands after touching the dough.

schedule.what: Make the dough balls. Build the pile twice. Measure the three balls each time. Add a hand press, and then write the three sentences.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, with every run and every mean. Draw a bar chart of the mean width for the three levels. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mean width of each dough ball after 5 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child rolling six small round balls of atta dough on a plate, each about the size of a big marble, beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Roll 6 balls of dough, each about 2 centimetres wide.

setup.art: A side view of a pile of eight books on a table, with a ball of dough between book 1 and book 2, one between book 4 and book 5, and one under book 8, each between two paper squares.
setup.caption: 2. Build the pile with dough at three levels, in a straight line.

setup.art: A child measuring the widest part of a squashed dough ball with a ruler, with the three squashed balls lined up in order beside the ruler.
setup.caption: 3. After 5 minutes, take the pile apart. Measure each ball.

flow.do: 1. Mix about 4 tablespoons of atta with 1 tablespoon of water. 2. Knead it for 2 minutes into a stiff dough. 3. Roll 6 balls, each about 2 centimetres wide. 4. Measure one ball and write down its width. 5. Cut the paper into 6 squares.
flow.say: We will make dough that shows how hard things press. First we need six balls that are all the same size. Make them stiff, not sticky.
flow.kid: Mix atta and a little water. Knead a stiff dough. Roll 6 balls, 2 cm wide each.
flow.parent: Stiff dough works best. If it sticks to your fingers, knead in more atta. Make a spare ball, because the trial in step 3 uses one.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dough Stack. Here you make the dough balls and the paper squares.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the eight books and the three levels: between book 1 and book 2, between book 4 and book 5, and under book 8. 2. Ask which ball will be squashed the widest. 3. Ask what a pressing hand will do to the bottom ball. 4. Write both guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: Each ball sits at a different level of the pile. Which one will be squashed the widest? Why do you think so? What will a hand pressing on top do to the bottom ball?
flow.kid: Guess which ball gets squashed the widest. Say why. Guess what a pressing hand does. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The bottom ball has more books on top of it.
The top ball only has one book pressing on it.
All the balls will be the same, because the books are the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Some children think the middle ball will be squashed most, or that all three will match, because all the books are equal.
flow.context: This step of the Dough Stack is for guessing. You guess before you build the pile.

flow.do: 1. Put a paper square on the table. 2. Put a ball on it, and another paper square on the ball. 3. Rest one book on top and wait 2 minutes. 4. Look at the ball. 5. If it is almost flat, use stiffer dough. If it has hardly changed, use softer dough.
flow.say: This is a trial with one ball and one book. The ball should spread a little in 2 minutes. If it does not, we change the dough before the real test.
flow.kid: Put one ball under one book for 2 minutes. Did it spread a little?
flow.parent: If the ball is flat under one book, the books are too heavy or the dough too soft. Knead in more atta. If nothing happens, add a few drops of water. Then use new balls for the real test.
flow.context: This step of the Dough Stack is a trial run. It checks that the dough is the right stiffness.

flow.do: 1. Put a paper square, a ball and another paper square on the table. 2. Lay book 8 on top. Then lay books 7, 6 and 5. 3. On book 5, put a square, a ball and a square in line with the first ball. 4. Lay books 4, 3 and 2. 5. On book 2, put a third square, ball and square. 6. Lay book 1 on top. Hold the pile steady for a moment. 7. Start the timer for 5 minutes.
flow.say: We build the pile from the bottom, with the three balls in a straight line. Keep the pile straight. Then we leave it alone for 5 minutes.
flow.kid: Build the pile from the bottom. Put a ball under book 8, book 4 and book 1. Wait 5 minutes.

ask.q: While you wait: how many books press down on each ball?
good: On the bottom ball, all eight.
On the middle ball, the top four.
On the top ball, only one.

flow.parent: Put each ball in the middle of its book. A grown-up should steady the pile while the child adds the next book. Do not press on the pile. While you wait, ask your child how hard each book is pressing.
flow.context: This is run 1 of the Dough Stack. Here you build the pile and wait 5 minutes.

flow.do: 1. After 5 minutes, lift off books 1 to 4 together and rest them on the table. 2. Peel the paper off the middle ball. Measure its widest part. 3. Lift off the other books. 4. Measure the bottom ball. 5. Measure the top ball too. Write all three down.
flow.say: After exactly 5 minutes we take the pile apart. We start from the top, so each ball keeps its squash. Measure the widest part of each ball.
flow.kid: Take the pile apart from the top. Measure the widest part of each ball. Write the widths down.
flow.parent: Measure to the nearest millimetre. Expect the bottom ball to be widest and the top ball narrowest. The balls are not perfectly round, so measure the widest part each time.
flow.context: This step of the Dough Stack is for measuring. Here you take the pile apart and measure each ball.

flow.do: 1. Make 3 new balls of the same size. 2. Build and measure the pile again, for run 2. 3. Write the widths in the table. 4. Find the mean of the two runs for each level.
flow.say: One run can be a fluke. So we build the pile again with new dough, and then take the mean of the two runs for each level.
flow.kid: Make 3 new balls. Build the pile again. Measure again. Find the mean for each level.
flow.parent: If run 2 gives a different order from run 1, look for the cause. Check that the balls started the same size and that you waited the same time.
flow.context: This is run 2 of the Dough Stack. Here you repeat the test with new dough.

flow.do: 1. Make 2 new balls. 2. Build a pile of eight books with one ball under book 8, and a plain sheet on top of book 1. 3. A grown-up presses gently on the top book with both hands for 2 minutes. The press is about as hard as pressing a bathroom scale to 5 kilograms. 4. Remove the books and measure the ball. 5. Compare it with the bottom ball from run 1.
flow.say: Now someone presses down on the pile. This is an applied force, a push from a hand. What will it do to the bottom ball?
flow.kid: A grown-up presses on the top book for 2 minutes. Measure the bottom ball. Is it wider?
flow.parent: A gentle, steady press is enough. The ball should end up a little wider than the bottom ball in run 1. If your first ball was already flat, the press may show little difference.
flow.context: This is part 2 of the Dough Stack. Here a hand presses on the pile, to add an applied force.

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar for each level in your table. 2. Ask your child for the three sentences. 3. Ask them to draw book 8 with its arrows. 4. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then draw the bottom book. Which arrows does it need?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why. Draw the bottom book with its arrows.

ask.q: Why was the bottom ball squashed the most, when all the books are the same?
good: It carried the weight of all eight books.
Each book rests on the one below, so the load grows towards the bottom.

ask.q: What did the hand do to the bottom ball?
good: It added its push to the weight of the books, so the ball spread more.

flow.parent: Expect widths that go up with the number of books above, but not in exact steps. Dough keeps flowing slowly, so the timing matters. The balls are measuring a push, in the way a bathroom scale does.

check.q: In the Dough Stack, the dough under book 8 was squashed the most. Why?
options: Book 8 is heavier than the others
It carried the weight of all eight books
Dough at the bottom is softer
check.why: All the books are the same weight. Each book rests on the one below it, so the load grows towards the bottom. The bottom ball carried eight books, and the top ball carried one. Choosing 'heavier' forgets that the books are equal.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Dough Stack. Here you explain your results and draw the arrows.

experiments.title: Lift, Press and Tilt: does a scale always read the weight?
experiments.context: In this experiment a 1 kilogram packet sits on a kitchen scale. You lift it with a string, press it with a finger and tilt the scale. The reading shows how hard the scale pushes up on the packet each time.
experiments.question: Does a scale always read the weight of the packet? What happens to its reading when the packet is lifted a little, pressed down, or put on a slope?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the reading go up, go down or stay the same when you lift the packet with a string? When you press it with a finger? When you tilt the scale? Write each guess and your reason. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same packet and the same scale for every part. Press the zero button with nothing on the scale, before each part. Hold each reading steady for 5 seconds before you write it down. Do each part 2 times, because one reading can be a fluke.
results_table: Extra force from you or the slope (newtons)

materials.item: a kitchen scale that reads in grams, up to 5 kilograms
a 1 kilogram packet of rice, sugar or dal, the shape of a flat pillow
about 60 centimetres of strong string or thick thread
a chopping board, a tray or a stiff board, about 40 centimetres long
books to lift one end of the board by 8, 14 and 20 centimetres
a ruler, sticky tape, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do the tilt part on a table, with a grown-up beside you. Then the scale and packet cannot fall on your foot. Lift the packet gently, because a thin string can cut your finger.

schedule.what: Weigh the packet. Lift it with the string, press it with a finger, and tilt the scale at three heights. Work out the extra forces and write the three sentences.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. In the last column write how much extra force you pulled up with, pressed down with, or what the slope took away. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: reading of a 1 kilogram packet on a kitchen scale
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A 1 kilogram packet with a loop of string round it standing on a kitchen scale, with the display showing about 1000 grams.
setup.caption: 1. Put the packet on the scale. Read it.

setup.art: A hand lifting the string loop so the packet is partly off the scale, and a second hand pressing one finger down on top of another packet on a scale.
setup.caption: 2. Lift the packet with the string. Then press it down with a finger.

setup.art: A kitchen scale on a chopping board that is tilted on a pile of books, with the packet on the scale held by a strip of tape across its lower edge.
setup.caption: 3. Put the scale on a tilted board and read it again.

flow.do: 1. Put the scale on a flat table and switch it on. 2. Press the zero button. 3. Lay the packet on the scale. 4. Write the reading in grams. 5. Divide it by 100 to get newtons, and write that too.
flow.say: A kitchen scale reads grams. 100 grams pulls down with about 1 newton. So we divide the reading by 100 to get newtons. This is the packet's weight.
flow.kid: Zero the scale. Put the packet on it. Write the reading. Divide by 100 for newtons.
flow.parent: Packets are never exactly 1 kilogram, so use whatever the scale reads. A reading of 1012 grams is about 10.1 newtons. This first reading is the weight to compare with the others.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lift, Press and Tilt. Here you find the packet's weight.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three changes: lifting with a string, pressing with a finger, and tilting. 2. Ask what the reading will do for each change. 3. Write the three guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: We will do three things to the packet. We will lift it a little, press it down, and tilt the scale. What will the reading do each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what the reading does for lifting, pressing and tilting. Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Lifting takes some weight off the scale, so it reads less.
Pressing adds a push, so it reads more.
A slope holds some of the packet up, so it reads less.

flow.parent: Many children say that the scale reads the weight every time. Do not correct this. The test will show it.
flow.context: This step of Lift, Press and Tilt is for guessing. You guess before you change anything.

flow.do: 1. Tie the string round the packet in a loop. 2. Zero the scale. 3. Put the packet on the scale. 4. Hold the loop and lift very slowly, until the scale reads about 700 grams. 5. Hold it steady for 5 seconds and write the reading. 6. Try reading 400 grams, and then lift it right off. 7. Work out your pull for each: 1000 minus the reading, divided by 100.
flow.say: Lift the packet slowly with the string. The scale now reads less. The packet's weight has not changed. So where did the missing push go? Work out how hard you are pulling.
flow.kid: Lift the packet with the string. Stop at 700 grams. Hold it still. Write the reading.

ask.q: The scale reads 700 grams. How hard is your string pulling up?
good: About 3 newtons, because 10 take away 7 is 3.
The packet's weight, 10, is shared between the scale, 7, and the string, 3.

flow.parent: A reading of 700 grams means the scale pushes up with 7 newtons. The string pulls up with 3 newtons. The two add up to the packet's 10 newtons. At 0 grams, the string carries it all.
flow.context: This is part 1 of Lift, Press and Tilt. Here you lift the packet with a string and watch the reading fall.

flow.do: 1. Put the packet back on the zeroed scale. 2. Press one finger gently on top of it, until the scale reads about 1500 grams. 3. Hold it steady for 5 seconds and write the reading. 4. Try again at about 2000 grams. 5. Work out your push for each: the reading minus 1000, divided by 100.
flow.say: Now press down on the packet with one finger. The scale reads more than the packet's weight. Work out how hard you are pressing.
flow.kid: Press one finger on the packet. Stop at 1500 grams. Hold it still. Write the reading.
flow.parent: A reading of 1500 grams means the scale pushes up with 15 newtons. The packet's weight is 10 and your finger adds 5. Press in a steady way. A jabbing press makes the reading jump.
flow.context: This is part 2 of Lift, Press and Tilt. Here you press the packet down and watch the reading rise.

flow.do: 1. Rest the board on the table with one end on a pile of books 8 centimetres high. 2. Put the scale on the board with sticky tape across its lower edge, to stop it sliding. 3. Press the zero button with the scale empty. 4. Lay the packet on the scale with a strip of tape across its lower edge. 5. Write the reading. 6. Repeat with the board raised 14 centimetres, and then 20 centimetres. Zero the scale each time.
flow.say: Now we tilt the scale. Zero it while it is empty and tilted, then put the packet on. The steeper the slope, the more of the packet's weight is held by the tape. What happens to the reading?
flow.kid: Tilt the board. Zero the empty scale. Put the packet on. Write the reading. Try 3 heights.
flow.parent: The packet should read about 980 grams at 8 centimetres, about 940 at 14 centimetres and about 870 at 20 centimetres. Some scales are not exact when tilted, so your numbers may differ by a few percent. Keep a hand near the scale. The tape across the lower edge holds the packet against sliding. It is not what the scale measures.
flow.context: This is part 3 of Lift, Press and Tilt. Here you tilt the scale and watch the reading fall as the slope gets steeper.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the last column of the table. 2. Draw a bar for each reading. 3. Ask your child for the three sentences.
flow.say: Look at your table. In which situations did the reading match the weight? In which was it bigger? In which was it smaller?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each reading. Which readings matched the weight?
flow.context: This step of Lift, Press and Tilt is for the table and the chart. Here you collect all the readings in one place.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask them to draw the packet on the scale with three arrows for the lifted case. 3. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then draw the packet while you lift it. Which three forces act on it?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why. Draw the lifted packet with 3 arrows.

ask.q: The scale read less than the weight when you lifted the packet. Why?
good: The string pulled up, so the scale did not need to push up as hard.
The scale only pushes as hard as it needs to, to hold the packet up with the string.

ask.q: Why did the reading fall on the tilted board?
good: The slope only stops the packet sinking into it, so the board pushes less than the weight.
The tape held the rest, along the slope.

flow.parent: A scale does not measure weight. It measures how hard the packet pushes on it. In the lifted case the three forces are gravity down, 10 newtons, the scale up, 7, and the string up, 3. Pressing and tilting follow the same idea.

check.q: In Lift, Press and Tilt, the scale read 700 grams while the packet hung partly from a string. What was the string pulling up with?
check.why: The packet's weight was about 10 newtons. The scale pushed up with 7. The string pulled up with the other 3, because 7 and 3 together make 10. Choosing 7 mixes up the scale's push with the string's pull.

flow.context: This is the last step of Lift, Press and Tilt. Here you explain your results and draw the forces.

experiments.title: The Spreading Square: why does a pull get weaker with distance?
experiments.context: In this experiment a small light shines through a square hole onto a screen. You move the screen further away and measure the lit square. It is a model for how the pull of a world spreads out and gets weaker.
experiments.question: When the screen is twice as far from the light, how much bigger is the lit square? And how bright is it, compared with before?
experiments.predict: Guess first. At twice the distance, the lit square could be twice as wide, twice the area or four times the area. Which will it be? Write your guess and your reason. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep the card with the square hole 10 centimetres from the light every time. Change only the distance from the light to the screen. Measure each lit square twice, from the same pencil marks, because the edges are a little fuzzy.
results_table: Area of the lit square (square cm)

materials.item: a phone torch (a small LED), or a small torch with no mirror round the bulb
a piece of thick card about 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres, with a 2 centimetre square hole cut in the middle
squared paper or a squared notebook page, taped flat on a wall as a screen
a tape measure or a metre ruler
books to rest the light on, sticky tape, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do not look straight into the light. A grown-up cuts the square hole. Do the test in a room with a curtain, in the evening, with one grown-up beside you.

schedule.what: Set up the light and the card. Mark the lit square at 30, 60 and 90 centimetres. Measure the sides, work out the areas and write the three sentences.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out each area by multiplying the side by itself. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: area of the lit square
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A phone torch lying on a pile of books, pointing at a wall, with a card that has a square hole standing 10 centimetres in front of it.
setup.caption: 1. Put the light on books. Stand the card with the hole 10 centimetres in front of it.

setup.art: A squared sheet taped to a wall, with a lit square on it, and a tape measure running from the light to the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Put the screen 30 centimetres from the light. Mark the lit square.

setup.art: Three squares drawn on one sheet, one small, one twice as wide and one three times as wide, with their sides labelled.
setup.caption: 3. Move the screen to 60 and 90 centimetres. Mark the square each time.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a 2 centimetre square hole in the middle of the card. 2. Tape the squared paper flat on a wall. 3. Rest the light on a pile of books so it shines at the paper. 4. Stand the card so that its hole is 10 centimetres from the light. 5. Make the room dark.
flow.say: The light spreads out in all directions. The card with the square hole lets only a square of light through. We will see how big that square is on the screen.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a square hole in the card. Tape up the paper. Stand the card 10 cm from the light.
flow.parent: A phone torch works well, because its light comes from one small point. A torch with a mirror behind the bulb makes a beam that does not spread in the same way. Fix the card so that it cannot move, with sticky tape on a book.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spreading Square. Here you set up the light, the card and the screen.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to look at the card and the wall. 2. Ask for a guess about the lit square at twice the distance. 3. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Suppose the lit square is 6 centimetres wide when the screen is 30 centimetres away. How big will it be at 60 centimetres? Twice as wide, twice the area, or four times the area? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how big the square will be at twice the distance. Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The square gets wider and also taller, so both sides double.
It doubles in width, and so it must be more than double in area.

flow.parent: Most children say 'twice as big'. Do not correct this. The sides of the square double, but the area is width times height.
flow.context: This step of the Spreading Square is for guessing. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: 1. Put the screen 30 centimetres from the light. 2. Mark the 4 corners of the lit square with a pencil. 3. Measure the side of the square. 4. Move the screen to 60 centimetres and mark the corners. 5. Move it to 90 centimetres and mark the corners. 6. Write the three sides in the table.
flow.say: Measure from the light to the screen with the tape. Mark the four corners of the lit square each time. Measure its side.
flow.kid: Put the screen at 30 cm. Mark the lit square. Do the same at 60 and 90 cm.
flow.parent: The edges are fuzzy, so mark where the light is clearly bright. At 30, 60 and 90 centimetres the sides should be about 6, 12 and 18 centimetres. Measure each side twice. If the squares are not square, the card is leaning.
flow.context: This step of the Spreading Square is for measuring. Here you mark the lit square at three distances.

flow.do: 1. Multiply each side by itself to get the area. 2. Divide each area by the area at 30 centimetres. 3. Write the answers in the table. 4. Look at how bright the square is at each distance.
flow.say: Work out the area of each square. Then work out how many times bigger each one is than the first. Look at the brightness too.
flow.kid: Multiply each side by itself. Divide by the first area. Write down the answers.
flow.parent: Expect the area to be about 4 times bigger at 60 centimetres and about 9 times bigger at 90. The light on the screen should be dimmer in the larger squares, because the same light covers more paper.
flow.context: This step of the Spreading Square is for the sums. Here you work out how the area grows.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask them to say how bright the light is at 60 centimetres, compared with 30. 3. Ask them how this might show what happens to the pull of a world. 4. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. If the same light covers 4 times the area, how bright is each part?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why. How bright is each part?

ask.q: At twice the distance, how bright is each part of the square?
good: One quarter as bright, because the same light covers 4 times the area.
