ask.q: The pull of a world also spreads out in all directions. What does that suggest for a thing twice as far from the centre?
good: Its pull would be one quarter as strong. At three times the distance, one ninth.

flow.parent: This is a model. Light and gravity are different things, but anything that spreads out evenly from a point follows the same sums. At twice the distance, the area of a sphere round the point is 4 times as big. Newton showed in 1687 that gravity follows this rule. Do not say that gravity is made of light.

check.q: In the Spreading Square, the screen moved from 30 to 90 centimetres. The distance was 3 times as big. How much bigger was the lit area?
check.why: The side of the square grew 3 times. The area is the side times itself, so it grew 3 times 3, which is 9 times. The same light covers 9 times the area, so each part is one ninth as bright. Choosing 3 forgets that the square grows in two directions.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Spreading Square. Here you explain your results.

activities.title: Be the Table: feel the push that holds a book up
activities.context: In this activity your own hand is the table. You hold books on your palm, add more books, and then someone presses down on them. You feel how a surface pushes up, and how that push has to grow.

materials.item: four books or thick notebooks of about the same size
a bed or a sofa to stand beside, in case a book falls
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Stand beside a bed, so that dropped books land on something soft. Stop when your arm is tired. A grown-up presses only gently.
activities.record: Draw your hand with one book on it. Draw one arrow for the push of your hand on the book, and one for the pull of gravity on the book. Say which arrow is longer when three books are on your hand.

setup.art: A child standing beside a bed with an arm stretched out flat and one book on the palm.
setup.caption: 1. Hold one book flat on your palm, with your arm straight.

setup.art: The same child with three books stacked on the palm and a grown-up's hand pressing down gently on the top book.
setup.caption: 2. Add books. Then a grown-up presses down gently on the top book.

setup.art: The same three books lying on a table with a small arrow pointing up from the table into the bottom book.
setup.caption: 3. Put the books on a table. The table pushes up too.

flow.do: 1. Stand beside the bed. 2. Hold one book flat on your open palm, with your arm out straight. 3. Count slowly to 10. 4. Notice which way your hand pushes.
flow.say: Hold the book on your palm. Your hand is the table. Which way is your hand pushing on the book? Which way is the book pushing on your hand?
flow.kid: Hold one book on your palm. Count to 10. Which way does your hand push?

ask.q: Which way does your hand push the book?
good: Up.
Up, as hard as the book pulls down.

ask.q: Which way does the book push your hand?
good: Down.
Down, into my palm.

flow.parent: The hand pushes up on the book, and the book pushes down on the hand, with equal strength. The Earth also pulls the book down. The book stays still because the hand's push balances that pull.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Table. Here your hand holds one book up.

flow.do: 1. Add a second book, and then a third. 2. Hold for 10 seconds each time. 3. Notice what your arm has to do as the books are added. 4. Put the books down when it feels hard.
flow.say: Add a second book, then a third. Your hand now has more to hold up. Does your hand have to push harder, or the same?
flow.kid: Add two more books, one at a time. Does your hand push harder?

ask.q: What does your hand have to do when you add books?
good: Push up harder.
Push up as hard as all the books weigh together.

flow.parent: The push must match the weight, or the books will fall. Your muscles do this without being told the number.
flow.context: This step of Be the Table adds more books. It shows how the push has to grow with the load.

flow.do: 1. Hold three books on your palm again. 2. A grown-up presses down gently on the top book with one hand. 3. Notice how your palm has to push. 4. The grown-up lets go.
flow.say: Now a grown-up presses gently on the top book. That is an applied force, a push from a hand. What does your palm have to do?
flow.kid: A grown-up presses on the top book. Does your palm push more or less?

ask.q: What did your palm have to do when the grown-up pressed down?
good: Push up harder, to hold up the weight and the push together.

flow.parent: Your palm has to push up with the weight of the books and the grown-up's press added together. Keep the press gentle.
flow.context: This step of Be the Table adds an applied force. A grown-up presses down on the books.

flow.do: 1. Put the three books on a table. 2. Ask if the table is pushing up on the books. 3. Ask why the table does not get tired. 4. Draw your hand and the books with two arrows.
flow.say: The table holds those same books for hours and does not get tired. Is the table pushing up on them? How can it, when it does not move?
flow.kid: Put the books on the table. Is the table pushing up? Why is it not tired?

ask.q: Is the table pushing up on the books?
good: Yes, because the books do not fall through it.
Yes, with the same force as your hand.

ask.q: Why does a table not get tired?
good: It is squashed by a tiny amount, and that squash is the push. It needs no energy to keep it.

flow.parent: A table does not use up energy to hold the books. It is squashed by a tiny amount, and its squashed particles push back. Your arm uses energy because muscles keep making small movements to hold the position.

check.q: You hold a book still on your palm. Which two forces on the book are equal?
options: Gravity pulling down and your palm pushing up
Your palm pushing up and the book pushing up
Gravity pulling down and gravity pulling up
check.why: The book is still, so the forces on it are balanced. Gravity pulls it down, and your palm pushes it up with the same force. The book also pushes down on your palm, but that is a force on your palm, not on the book.

flow.context: This is the last step of Be the Table. Here the table takes over from your hand.

activities.title: Weigh Yourself on Nine Worlds
activities.context: In this activity you find your own mass on a bathroom scale. Then you multiply it by the strength of gravity on each world, to find your weight there. You draw the weights as bars.

materials.item: a bathroom scale that reads in kilograms (or use the mass on a school health card, or use 30 kilograms)
a calculator
squared paper, a ruler, a pencil and a notebook

activities.record: Make a table of 9 worlds with the strength of gravity and your weight there. Draw a bar chart of your weight on each world. Write one sentence on which world surprised you.

setup.art: A child standing on a bathroom scale that reads 32 kilograms, with a notebook in hand.
setup.caption: 1. Find your mass on a bathroom scale.

setup.art: A table with nine rows: Moon, Mercury, Mars, Venus, Uranus, Earth, Saturn, Neptune and Jupiter, with the strength of gravity beside each.
setup.caption: 2. Multiply your mass by the strength of gravity for each world.

setup.art: A bar chart with nine bars of different heights, and the Earth bar marked in a different colour.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar for each world.

flow.do: 1. Stand on the bathroom scale. 2. Read your mass in kilograms, to the nearest kilogram. 3. Write it down. 4. If you have no scale, use the mass on a school health card, or use 30 kilograms.
flow.say: This is your mass. It is the amount of matter in you. It will be the same on every world. Write it down.
flow.kid: Stand on the scale. Read your mass in kilograms. Write it down.
flow.parent: A bathroom scale marked in kilograms really measures a push. It shows that push as a mass, using the Earth's strength of gravity. That is why it only works on Earth. For this activity, its number is your mass.
flow.context: This is the first step of Nine Worlds. Here you find your mass.

flow.do: 1. Show the table of the strength of gravity. 2. Moon 1.6, Mercury 3.7, Mars 3.7, Venus 8.9, Uranus 8.9. 3. Earth 9.8, Saturn 10.4, Neptune 11.2, Jupiter 25. 4. Ask which world will make your weight the biggest, and which the smallest.
flow.say: These numbers say how many newtons one kilogram weighs on each world. Which world will make you weigh the most? Which the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the numbers. Guess which world makes you heaviest. Guess the lightest. Say why.

ask.q: Which world do you think will give the biggest weight, and why?
good: Jupiter, because it is the biggest planet.
Jupiter, because its number is 25, the biggest in the table.

flow.parent: Some children think Saturn gives the biggest weight, because it is the next biggest planet. Do not correct this yet. The bar chart in step 4 shows the surprise.
flow.context: This step of Nine Worlds is for guessing. You guess before you do the sums.

flow.do: 1. Multiply your mass by the number for each world. 2. Write each answer in newtons in the table. 3. For example, a mass of 32 kilograms on the Moon gives 32 times 1.6, which is 51 newtons. 4. Do all nine worlds with the calculator.
flow.say: Multiply your mass by each number. This works because the number says how many newtons one kilogram weighs. The answer is your weight there, in newtons.
flow.kid: Multiply your mass by each number. Write the nine answers in newtons.
flow.parent: Check one answer by hand. Mass 32 on Earth gives 32 times 9.8, which is about 314 newtons. Round to the nearest newton. Saturn and Jupiter have no solid surface, so their numbers are for the top of their clouds.
flow.context: This step of Nine Worlds is for the sums. Here you work out your weight on nine worlds.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, draw a bar for each world. 2. Let 1 square stand for 20 newtons. 3. Colour the Earth bar. 4. Mark which bars are taller than Earth's, and which are shorter.
flow.say: Draw a bar for your weight on each world. Let one square stand for 20 newtons. Colour the Earth bar, so that you can compare.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each world. Colour Earth's bar. Which bars are taller?
flow.parent: Saturn's bar is a little taller than Earth's. Uranus and Venus are a little shorter. Jupiter's is the tallest by far, about two and a half times Earth's.
flow.context: This step of Nine Worlds is for the bar chart. Here you draw your weight on all nine worlds.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child which world surprised them. 2. Ask whether a grown-up's bars would be taller or shorter than theirs. 3. Ask what a bathroom scale in kilograms would read on the Moon. 4. Write one sentence on each answer.
flow.say: Which bar surprised you? Would a grown-up's bars be taller or shorter than yours? What would your bathroom scale read on the Moon?
flow.kid: Which bar surprised you? What would the bathroom scale read on the Moon?

ask.q: Would a grown-up's bars be taller or shorter?
good: Taller, because a grown-up has more mass.
Taller on every world, in the same pattern.

ask.q: What would a bathroom scale marked in kilograms read on the Moon?
good: About one sixth of the number on Earth.
It measures a push, and the Moon pulls about 6 times less.

flow.parent: The bars follow the same pattern for everybody, because weight is mass times a number for the world. A scale marked in kilograms is set for the Earth's pull. So on the Moon it would read about one sixth as much.

check.q: A girl weighs 300 newtons on Earth. About what does she weigh on Mars, where the number is 3.7?
check.why: Her mass is about 30 kilograms, because 300 divided by 10 is 30. On Mars, 30 times 3.7 is 111 newtons. Choosing 300 forgets that weight changes from world to world.

flow.context: This is the last step of Nine Worlds. Here you think about what the bars show.

activities.title: Hit the Bottles: the same hit on a full and a nearly empty bottle
activities.context: In this activity a small ball swings into a hanging bottle. First the bottle is full of water, and then it is nearly empty. You see how far each bottle swings, to find out what mass does when no weight needs holding up.

materials.item: a 1 litre plastic bottle with its cap
water, to fill the bottle and then to leave 100 millilitres in it
a broom handle or long stick, rested across the backs of two heavy chairs
about 1 metre of string, cut into two pieces of 40 centimetres
a tennis ball, or a lime, with a loop of tape to tie the string to
a ruler, sticky tape, a pencil and a notebook

activities.safety: A grown-up checks that the stick cannot slip off the chairs. Stand to the side, not under the bottle. Wipe up any spilt water at once.
activities.record: Draw the full bottle with one arrow for the pull of the string and one for gravity. Write how far each bottle swung, and what you think that shows.

setup.art: A broom handle resting across two chairs, with a bottle and a ball hanging side by side from short strings so that they just touch.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the full bottle and the ball so that they just touch.

setup.art: A child pulling the ball back 20 centimetres from the bottle, with a ruler beside it, ready to let go.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the ball back 20 centimetres and let it go.

setup.art: A helper holding a ruler level behind the hanging bottle, with a finger on the place the bottle reached.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far the bottle swings.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle to the top and put the cap on. 2. Tie a 40 centimetre string round the bottle's neck, below the cap ring. 3. Tie the other string to the ball with the tape. 4. Hang the bottle and the ball from the stick, side by side, so that they just touch.
flow.say: A string carries the weight of the bottle. So weight is not the question here. We want to know what the mass does when a ball hits the bottle sideways.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle. Hang it and the ball from the stick. They should just touch.
flow.parent: The full bottle has a mass of about 1 kilogram. The strings should hang straight down. The ball should touch the bottle at its middle. A grown-up should check that the stick is safe on the chairs.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hit the Bottles. Here you hang the full bottle and the ball.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child you will test a nearly empty bottle later, with 100 millilitres of water. 2. Ask which bottle will swing further when the same ball hits it. 3. Ask why. 4. Write the guess.
flow.say: The ball will hit a full bottle now, and a nearly empty one later. Which bottle will swing further? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which bottle will swing further. Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The empty one is lighter, so it is easier to move.
The full one is heavier, so the ball cannot move it much.

flow.parent: Most children guess correctly. Ask for the reason. Then see whether it is about weight or about something else.
flow.context: This step of Hit the Bottles is for guessing. You guess before you swing the ball.

flow.do: 1. Pull the ball back until it is 20 centimetres from the bottle, measured sideways. 2. Let go without a push. 3. Ask a helper to hold a ruler level beside the bottle and watch how far it swings. 4. Do this 3 times and write each distance. 5. Catch the bottle after each hit.
flow.say: Pull the ball back 20 centimetres. Let it go. The ball hits the bottle. Measure how far the bottle swings away.
flow.kid: Pull the ball back 20 cm. Let it go. Measure how far the full bottle swings.
flow.parent: Do not push the ball. Use the same distance every time. The full bottle may swing only 1 or 2 centimetres. You can film the swing with a phone and look at it again. Catch the bottle, so that it does not swing back into the ball.
flow.context: This step of Hit the Bottles tests the full bottle. The ball hits it three times.

flow.do: 1. Pour out the water until only 100 millilitres is left. Put the cap on. 2. Hang the bottle in the same place. 3. Use the same ball and the same 20 centimetre distance. 4. Do it 3 times and write each distance. 5. Find the mean for each bottle.
flow.say: Now the nearly empty bottle gets the same hit. Use the same place and the same distance. How far does it swing, compared with the full bottle?
flow.kid: Pour most of the water out. Hit the bottle three times. Measure how far it swings.
flow.parent: Expect the nearly empty bottle to swing about 4 to 6 times as far. The exact number depends on the ball and the string. The ball gives both bottles the same hit, and they respond differently.
flow.context: This step of Hit the Bottles tests the nearly empty bottle. The same ball hits it in the same way.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. 2. Ask what made the full bottle hard to move, since a string held up its weight. 3. Ask what would happen on the Moon. 4. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. A string held the weight of the bottle. So what made the full one hard to move?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why. What made the full one hard to move?

ask.q: What made the full bottle hard to move sideways?
good: It has more mass, and mass makes a thing hard to start moving.
More mass means more inertia.

ask.q: Would the results differ on the Moon?
good: No. The ball would give the same hit, and the bottle would respond in the same way. Mass is the same there.

flow.parent: Mass has a second job besides setting weight. It decides how hard a thing is to start moving or stop. This is called inertia, and it does not depend on gravity. A full bottle on the Moon would still be hard to swing.

check.q: A string holds up both bottles, so weight is not the difference. Why did the full bottle swing less?
options: It has more mass, so it is harder to start moving
It is pulled harder by gravity, so it cannot swing
check.why: The string carries the weight of the bottle. The sideways hit meets only the mass, which decides how hard the bottle is to start moving. Choosing gravity mixes up weight, which is held by the string, with inertia, which is about mass.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hit the Bottles. Here you explain what mass does.

activities.title: Arrows to Scale: weigh it, then draw the forces
activities.context: In this activity you weigh a packet and a book on a kitchen scale. You turn the grams into newtons and draw force arrows with a scale of 1 centimetre for each newton. You check that the arrows balance.

materials.item: a kitchen scale in grams
a 500 gram packet of rice or sugar, and a book
squared paper, a ruler, coloured pencils and a notebook

activities.record: Keep your five diagrams on squared paper, with the scale written beside each one. Under each, write the total of the up arrows and the total of the down arrows.

setup.art: A kitchen scale with a 500 gram packet on it and a notebook beside it with the number 5 newtons written.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh the packet and the book. Divide by 100 for newtons.

setup.art: A squared paper page with a box and two arrows of equal length, one pointing down and one pointing up.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the forces on the packet, with 1 centimetre for each newton.

setup.art: The same page with a second box where a finger presses down, and the up arrow is longer than the down arrow.
setup.caption: 3. Draw four more cases. Check that the arrows balance.

flow.do: 1. Weigh the packet on the kitchen scale. 2. Divide the grams by 100 to get newtons. 3. Weigh the book and do the same. 4. Write both weights.
flow.say: A scale reads grams. 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. So we divide by 100. A 500 gram packet weighs about 5 newtons.
flow.kid: Weigh the packet and the book. Divide the grams by 100. Write the newtons.
flow.parent: Use the real readings. If the book is 320 grams, its weight is about 3.2 newtons. The scale for the drawings is 1 centimetre for each newton.
flow.context: This is the first step of Arrows to Scale. Here you find the weight of two things.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, draw the packet as a small box. 2. Draw a gravity arrow down from its middle, as many centimetres long as its newtons. 3. Draw a normal force arrow up from its base, the same length. 4. Label both and write the scale.
flow.say: Draw the packet resting on a table. Draw gravity down. Draw the table's push up. How long should each arrow be, with 1 centimetre for each newton?
flow.kid: Draw the packet on a table. Draw gravity down. Draw the table's push up, as long.

ask.q: Why are the two arrows the same length?
good: The packet stays still, so the forces on it are balanced.
The table pushes up as hard as gravity pulls down.

flow.parent: The gravity arrow starts at the middle of the packet. The normal force arrow starts at the surface where the packet touches the table. Each has the same length, 5 centimetres.
flow.context: This step of Arrows to Scale is the first diagram. A packet rests on a table.

flow.do: 1. Draw the packet again. 2. This time a finger presses down on it with 2 newtons. 3. Draw the finger's arrow 2 centimetres long. 4. Work out the table's push: the weight plus the press. 5. Draw the normal force arrow that long.
flow.say: Now a finger presses down with 2 newtons. What must the table push with? Draw the arrows with 1 centimetre for each newton.
flow.kid: Draw the packet with a finger pressing down. How long is the table's arrow now?

ask.q: How big is the table's push when the finger presses with 2 newtons?
good: 7 newtons, because 5 plus 2 is 7.

flow.parent: The down arrows are gravity, 5, and the finger, 2. The up arrow is 7. Check that the total up equals the total down.
flow.context: This step of Arrows to Scale is the second diagram. A finger presses on the packet.

flow.do: 1. Draw a third diagram, of the packet hanging from a string. 2. Draw gravity down, 5 centimetres. 3. Draw the string's pull up, 5 centimetres. 4. Draw a fourth diagram, of the book on a table. 5. Draw a fifth, of three books in a pile. Draw the forces on the middle book only.
flow.say: Draw three more. The hanging packet needs two arrows. The book on the table needs two. The middle book in a pile of three needs three arrows. Which three?
flow.kid: Draw the hanging packet. Draw the book on a table. Draw the middle of three books.

ask.q: What three forces act on the middle book of three?
good: Gravity down, the push of the top book down, and the push of the bottom book up.
The up arrow is as long as the two down arrows together.

flow.parent: For the middle book, say it weighs 3 newtons. Gravity is 3 down, the top book pushes 3 down, and the bottom book pushes 6 up. The rule is the same for every diagram. If the thing stays still, the up arrows must equal the down arrows.
flow.context: This step of Arrows to Scale holds diagrams three to five. They show a hanging packet, a book and a pile.

flow.do: 1. Check each diagram. 2. Add the up arrows, and add the down arrows. 3. Write both totals under each one. 4. Ask your child what the totals show.
flow.say: Add up the arrows going up and the arrows going down in each diagram. What do you notice about the two totals?
flow.kid: Add the up arrows and the down arrows. What do you notice about the totals?

ask.q: What do the totals show?
good: They are equal, because each thing stays still.
A thing that stays still has balanced forces.

flow.parent: If a diagram does not balance, check the arithmetic first. Then look for a missing force, such as a hand or a string.

check.q: A 3 newton book rests on a table. A finger presses down on it with 2 newtons. How long is the table's arrow, with 1 centimetre for each newton?
check.why: The table must push up against the book's weight and the finger's press together. 3 plus 2 is 5 newtons, so the arrow is 5 centimetres. Choosing 3 leaves out the finger's press.

flow.context: This is the last step of Arrows to Scale. Here you check that the forces balance.

activities.title: Pull Detective: work out the strength of gravity from mass and width
activities.context: In this activity you use the mass and the width of each world to work out the pull at its surface. Then you check your answers against the table from Nine Worlds.

materials.item: a calculator
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with one row for each world. Write the mass, the width, the width times the width, the mass divided by that, and the answer times 9.8. Write a sentence on what surprised you.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table whose columns are: mass, width, width times width, mass divided by that, and strength of gravity.
setup.caption: 1. Make a table with five columns.

setup.art: A calculator beside the table, with the Moon's row filled in: 0.0123, 0.273, 0.0745, 0.165 and 1.6.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the Moon's row.

setup.art: A completed table with Saturn's row circled, showing a number close to the Earth's.
setup.caption: 3. Do the other worlds. Circle the one that surprises you.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table with a row for each world. 2. Copy the mass and the width of each world. 3. Moon 0.0123 and 0.273. Mars 0.107 and 0.532. Venus 0.815 and 0.949. Uranus 14.5 and 4.01. 4. Neptune 17.1 and 3.88. Saturn 95.2 and 9.45. Jupiter 318 and 11.2.
flow.say: Every world is compared with the Earth. The Earth counts as 1 for its mass and 1 for its width. So Jupiter's mass of 318 means 318 times the Earth's.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Copy the masses and widths. The Earth is 1 and 1.
flow.parent: The numbers say how many times the Earth's mass and width each world has. They are rounded from NASA's planetary fact sheets.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pull Detective. Here you set up the table of masses and widths.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess which world has the strongest pull at its surface. 2. Ask which worlds pull less than the Earth. 3. Write the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: Jupiter has the most mass of all. So does it have the strongest pull at its surface? Why do you think so? Which worlds might pull less than the Earth?
flow.kid: Guess which world pulls hardest. Guess which pull less than Earth. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: More mass means more pull.
Distance from the centre matters too, so a very wide planet might pull less.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the planet with more mass to pull harder. The next step tests that.
flow.context: This step of Pull Detective is for guessing. You guess before you do the sums.

flow.do: 1. For the Moon, multiply 0.273 by 0.273. 2. Divide 0.0123 by that answer. 3. Multiply by 9.8. 4. Write the answer. 5. Do Mars, Venus and Neptune the same way.
flow.say: Here is the sum. Multiply the width by itself. Divide the mass by that number. Multiply by 9.8. The answer is the strength of gravity, in newtons for each kilogram.
flow.kid: Width times width. Mass divided by that. Then times 9.8. Do the Moon first.
flow.parent: The answers should be about 1.6 for the Moon, 3.7 for Mars, 8.9 for Venus and 11 for Neptune. Small differences are fine, because the table is rounded. The width counts twice, because the pull gets weaker with the square of the distance.
flow.context: This step of Pull Detective is the sum. You work out the strength of gravity for four worlds.

flow.do: 1. Do the sum for Uranus, Saturn and Jupiter. 2. Write each answer. 3. Compare your answers with the table in Nine Worlds. 4. Circle the world with the biggest surprise.
flow.say: Now Uranus, Saturn and Jupiter. Check each answer against the table. Which world surprised you most?
flow.kid: Do Uranus, Saturn and Jupiter. Compare with the table. Circle the surprise.

ask.q: Saturn has 95 times the Earth's mass. Why is its pull about the same as the Earth's?
good: Its cloud tops are very far from its centre, so its mass pulls much less there.
Distance from the centre counts twice.

flow.parent: Expect Uranus about 8.8, Saturn about 10.4 and Jupiter about 25. Saturn has 95 times the Earth's mass, yet its pull is close to the Earth's. Uranus pulls a little less than the Earth.
flow.context: This step of Pull Detective finishes the sums. You check them against the table from Nine Worlds.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what the sum is doing. 2. Ask what would happen to the pull if a planet kept its mass but became twice as wide. 3. Write the answer.
flow.say: If a planet kept its mass but grew twice as wide, what would happen to the pull on its surface? Use the sum to find out.
flow.kid: A planet has the same mass but twice the width. What happens to its pull?

ask.q: What happens to the pull if the width doubles and the mass stays the same?
good: It becomes one quarter, because 2 times 2 is 4 and we divide by 4.

flow.parent: This links to the Spreading Square, where doubling the distance made the light spread over 4 times the area.

check.q: A planet has the same mass as the Earth, but is three times as wide. How strong is the pull at its surface, compared with the Earth?
check.why: The pull is the mass divided by the width times the width. Three times as wide gives 3 times 3, which is 9. So the pull is one ninth as strong. Choosing one third forgets that the width counts twice.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pull Detective. Here you use the sum to answer a new question.

projects.title: The Load on the Pillar: how much weight does a ground-floor pillar carry?
projects.context: In this three-day project you choose one pillar on the ground floor of a block of flats or another building. You measure the floor it holds up, estimate the mass above it and work out the force the ground must push back with.

materials.item: a measuring tape or a long piece of string and a ruler
a calculator
a notebook and a pencil
a grown-up to come with you

projects.safety: Stay at ground level, in the parking area, a corridor or the compound. Do not climb, and do not touch electric boxes or cables. A grown-up stays with you the whole time.

schedule.what: Count the floors. Choose a pillar. Measure its width and the distance to the next pillars.
Work out the floor area the pillar holds up, the mass above it and its weight in newtons.
Compare the load on a ground-floor pillar and a top-floor pillar. Draw the load path and write the three sentences.

projects.record: Write the number of floors, the pillar's width, the area it holds up, the mass above it and its weight in newtons. Draw the load path from the roof to the Earth, with arrows that grow longer towards the bottom.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and a tape measure beside a concrete pillar in the parking area of a block of flats, looking up at the floors above.
setup.caption: 1. Count the floors. Measure the pillar and the gaps.

setup.art: A plan drawn from above, with a pillar in the middle of a rectangle and the neighbouring pillars at the corners.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the floor area that the pillar holds up.

setup.art: A tall column of arrows that get longer towards the bottom, from the roof through each floor and the pillar into the ground.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the load path, with the arrows growing towards the ground.

flow.do: 1. Go with a grown-up to the ground floor of a building with at least three floors. 2. Count the floors above the ground, and count the roof as one more floor. 3. Choose one pillar. 4. Measure the pillar's width. 5. Measure the distance to the next pillar on each side. 6. Draw a plan from above and write the numbers on it.
flow.say: A pillar holds up all the floors above it. Let's choose one pillar and measure it. We also measure how far it is from its neighbours.
flow.kid: Count the floors. Choose a pillar. Measure its width. Measure the gaps to the next pillars.
flow.parent: Choose a pillar with other pillars around it in a grid. If the building has walls instead of pillars, choose a stretch of wall and measure 1 metre of it. Stay on the ground floor. Pace out long distances and check one pace with a tape.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Load on the Pillar. Here you count the floors and measure one pillar.

flow.do: 1. Multiply the two gaps to find the floor area the pillar holds up, in square metres. 2. Multiply the area by the number of floors. 3. Multiply by 1,000 kilograms. A rough rule gives one square metre of one floor a mass of about 1,000 kilograms. This counts its walls, furniture and people. 4. Multiply the mass by 10 to get its weight in newtons.
flow.say: Engineers use a rough rule. One square metre of one floor has a mass of about 1,000 kilograms. We multiply by the area and the number of floors. This is a guess, but it is a good one.
flow.kid: Multiply the two gaps for the area. Multiply by the floors. Multiply by 1,000 kilograms. Then by 10 for newtons.

ask.q: Suppose a pillar holds up 20 square metres on each of 6 floors. What is the mass above it?
good: 20 times 6 is 120 square metres, and 120 times 1,000 is 120,000 kilograms.
Its weight is about 1,200,000 newtons.

flow.parent: A worked example: gaps of 4 metres and 5 metres give 20 square metres. With 6 floors, that is 120 square metres, 120,000 kilograms, or about 1,200,000 newtons. That is about 6 loaded lorries. Real engineers add up every beam, wall and load exactly. This rule only gives the right size of answer.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Load on the Pillar. Here you work out the mass above the pillar and its weight.

flow.do: 1. Work out the load on a top-floor pillar, with only the roof above it. 2. Divide the ground-floor load by the top-floor load. 3. Draw the load path from the roof down to the ground. 4. Draw an arrow at each floor, longer as you go down. 5. Write the three sentences.
flow.say: The top-floor pillar has only the roof above it. How many times bigger is the load on the ground-floor pillar? Draw the load path from the roof to the ground.
flow.kid: Work out the top pillar's load. How many times bigger is the bottom one? Draw the load path.

ask.q: Where does the load end up?
good: In the ground, which pushes back up under the pillar.
In the end the Earth holds it.

ask.q: Why are the lower pillars often thicker?
good: They carry more floors.

flow.parent: With 6 floors, the ground-floor pillar carries 6 times the load of the top-floor pillar. Some buildings still use the same pillar size all the way up. The thicker steel inside the lower pillars is hidden. Ask a building engineer or look at the plans if you can.

check.q: A pillar on the ground floor holds up 6 floors. A pillar on the top floor holds up only the roof. How do their loads compare?
options: The ground-floor pillar carries 6 times as much
check.why: Each floor adds the same load, and the ground-floor pillar carries every floor above it. So its load is 6 times the load at the top, if the floor areas are the same. Choosing equal forgets that loads are passed down and add up.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Load on the Pillar. Here you compare the loads and draw the path of the load.

challenges.title: The Three-Storey Paper Tower: put the strength where the load is
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Dough Stack, the load grew towards the bottom of the pile. Here you build a three-storey tower from paper tubes. Each floor carries a load, so the bottom storey must be the strongest.
challenges.problem: Build a tower of three storeys from paper tubes and stiff card floors. Every floor must carry one load without the tubes crumpling. Use the fewest tubes you can.
constraints: Each storey is 8 centimetres tall, and each tube is rolled from one strip of paper, 8 centimetres wide.
Each floor is a card square of about 25 centimetres. A load lies on each floor, and no load may touch a tube.
You may use at most 6 sheets of paper, which make 12 strips, and sticky tape.
materials: 6 sheets of A4 paper, each cut into 2 strips of 8 centimetres by 29.7 centimetres
stiff card from a cereal box, cut into 4 squares of 25 centimetres
3 equal loads, such as 1 kilogram packets of rice or dal, or 1 litre bottles of water, or thick books
general: Use the same number of tubes in every storey, for example 3 in each. This holds, but it wastes tubes in the top storeys.
Use bigger tubes at the bottom. This also works, but a big tube is only as good as how well it is taped.
creative: Count the floors above each storey. Use 1 tube in the top storey, 2 in the middle and 3 in the bottom. Then every tube carries the same load.
Put the tubes at the corners of each floor and the load in the middle, so that the floor does not bend.
Try a different shape for the tubes. A tube rolled into a triangle may hold more than a round tube of the same paper.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own tower with four floors and 10 strips. Draw it and say how many tubes go in each storey, and why. Then build it and test it. Did every storey hold? Which storey was nearest to crumpling?

setup.art: A child rolling a paper strip into a tube and taping it, with several finished tubes beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Roll each strip into a tube, 8 centimetres tall, and tape it.

setup.art: A single paper tube standing on a table with a card square on top and one 1 kilogram packet resting on the card.
setup.caption: 2. Test one tube alone, with 1, 2 and 3 loads on top.

setup.art: A three-storey tower with 3 tubes in the bottom storey, 2 in the middle and 1 in the top, and a packet on each card floor.
setup.caption: 3. Build the tower with more tubes at the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Cut the paper into 12 strips. 2. Roll each strip into a tube, 8 centimetres tall. 3. Tape the tube along its edge. 4. Stand one tube on the table, with a card square on top. 5. Lay the loads on the card one at a time. Write how many it holds before it crumples.
flow.say: First we find out how strong one tube is. We add loads one at a time. How many does a single tube hold before it crumples?
flow.kid: Roll 12 tubes. Stand one up with a card on top. Add loads one at a time.
flow.parent: Stand beside the table, in case the tower falls. Test the tube once only, because a crumpled tube is weaker. If one tube holds more than 3 loads, roll the tubes from newspaper instead, because it is thinner. If it crumples under one load, tape a second layer round it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three-Storey Paper Tower. Here you test how many loads one tube can hold.

flow.do: 1. Build the tower with 3 tubes in every storey, as the general solution says. 2. Put a load on each floor. 3. Watch each storey for 10 seconds. 4. Write which storey, if any, bends or crumples first.
flow.say: Our first tower uses the same number of tubes in every storey. We put one load on each floor. Which storey is under the most strain? Which tubes will crumple first, if any?
flow.kid: Build the tower with 3 tubes in each storey. Put a load on each floor. Which storey is in trouble?

ask.q: Which storey carries the most, and how many loads does it carry?
good: The bottom storey, which carries all 3 loads.
The top storey carries only 1.

flow.parent: This tower should hold. But the top tubes carry far less than they could. Ask your child which tubes were working hardest.
flow.context: This step of the Three-Storey Paper Tower tests the first design. Every storey has the same number of tubes.

flow.do: 1. Take the tower down. 2. Count the floors above each storey, including its own. 3. Rebuild with 1 tube in the top storey, 2 in the middle and 3 in the bottom. 4. Put a load on each floor. 5. Does every storey hold?
flow.say: Count the loads that each storey carries. The top carries 1, the middle 2 and the bottom 3. So we use 1, 2 and 3 tubes. Then every tube carries the same load.
flow.kid: Take the tower down. Rebuild it with 1, 2 and 3 tubes. Put a load on each floor.
flow.parent: This design uses 6 tubes, half as many as the first. Each tube carries about 1 load. If a tube crumples, tape its top and bottom edges. You can also add one tube to that storey.

check.q: A tower has 4 floors, and each carries one load. How many loads does the bottom storey carry?
check.why: The bottom storey carries its own floor and all the floors above it. With 4 floors, that is 4 loads. Choosing 1 forgets that loads are passed down and add up.

flow.context: This step of the Three-Storey Paper Tower tests the creative design. The tubes go 1, 2 and 3 from top to bottom.

flow.do: 1. Plan your own tower with 4 floors and 10 strips. 2. Draw it, and write how many tubes go in each storey. 3. Say why. 4. Build it and test it. 5. Write which storey, if any, crumpled.
flow.say: Now plan your own tower with four floors and ten strips. Draw it first. Say how many tubes go in each storey, and why. Then test it.
flow.kid: Plan a tower with 4 floors and 10 strips. Draw it. Build it. Test it.
flow.parent: The pattern 1, 2, 3 and 4 uses exactly 10 strips. Real buildings do the same in steel and concrete, and engineers also add a safety margin. If you changed the design, ask what you were trying to improve.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Three-Storey Paper Tower. Here you design, build and test your own tower.

challenges.title: The 50-Newton Pack: how much can you carry on each world?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A pack that weighs 50 newtons on Earth has a mass of about 5 kilograms. On another world, the same 50 newtons holds a different mass. You work out what to pack for a trip, and see what does not change.
challenges.problem: You can carry a pack that weighs no more than 50 newtons on the world you visit. Choose what to take from the list. You must take water and a tent. Find the best pack for the Moon and for Mars. Then say whether the trip works at Jupiter's cloud tops.
constraints: The pack may not weigh more than 50 newtons on that world.
You must take the tent, 4 kilograms, and water, 3 kilograms.
You may also choose from these, with their masses: sleeping bag 2 kilograms, food for 2 days 2 kilograms, camera and panel 3 kilograms.
More to choose from: rock hammer and tools 4 kilograms, first aid kit 1 kilogram, rope 3 kilograms, ladder 5 kilograms, spare battery 6 kilograms.
materials: 5 bottles of 1 litre water, a strong bag, and a kitchen scale (to feel what 50 newtons is)
general: On Earth the limit is about 5 kilograms, but the tent and the water already have a mass of 7 kilograms. So the trip cannot be done on Earth.
On the Moon the limit is about 31 kilograms, so you can take almost everything on the list.
creative: Use a cart. The ground carries the weight of a cart. Your arms only have to push it to make it go.
Share the pack between two people. Each carries 50 newtons, so the team carries twice the mass.
Leave behind what you can make or find, such as rocks to weigh down the tent.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose a world from the table of Nine Worlds. Work out the limit for a 50 newton pack there. Choose your pack and write its total mass. Then say what will be hard about turning round with it.

setup.art: A child carrying a strong bag with five bottles of water, with a small arrow labelled 50 newtons pulling down on the bag.
setup.caption: 1. Carry 5 bottles of water in a bag. That is about 50 newtons on Earth.

setup.art: A table with the worlds, the strength of gravity and the limit in kilograms for a 50 newton pack.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the limit for each world.

setup.art: A list of items with their masses, and ticks beside the ones chosen for the Moon pack.
setup.caption: 3. Choose your pack.

flow.do: 1. Put 5 one litre bottles of water in a strong bag. 2. Carry it across the room and feel how heavy it is. 3. Check its mass on a kitchen scale if you can. 4. Write it down. This pack weighs about 50 newtons on Earth.
flow.say: Carry this bag. Five bottles of water have a mass of about 5 kilograms, and weigh about 50 newtons. That is the pull we can carry for the whole trip.
flow.kid: Put 5 bottles in a bag. Carry it. This is about 50 newtons.
flow.parent: Use a bag with strong handles. A child of 10 can usually carry 5 kilograms for a few minutes. Stop if it is too heavy.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 50-Newton Pack. Here you feel what 50 newtons is like.

flow.do: 1. For each world, divide 50 by the strength of gravity. 2. The Moon is 50 divided by 1.6, which is about 31 kilograms. 3. Mars is 50 divided by 3.7. 4. Jupiter's cloud tops are 50 divided by 25. 5. Write all three limits. 6. Check whether the tent and water fit under each limit.
flow.say: The pack must weigh 50 newtons or less. So we divide 50 by the strength of gravity. That gives the most mass we can carry on that world.
flow.kid: Divide 50 by the number for each world. Write the limits in kilograms. Do the tent and water fit?

ask.q: Why does dividing by the strength of gravity give the mass?
good: Weight is mass times the strength of gravity, so mass is weight divided by it.

flow.parent: The limits are about 31 kilograms on the Moon, 13.5 on Mars and 2 on Jupiter's cloud tops. The tent and water have a mass of 7 kilograms, so the trip fails on Jupiter. It has no ground to stand on anyway.
flow.context: This step of the 50-Newton Pack is the sum. Here you find the most mass you could carry on each world.

flow.do: 1. Choose items for the Moon pack, with the tent and water. 2. Add up their masses. 3. Check that the total is 31 kilograms or less. 4. Do the same for Mars. 5. Write both lists, and the total mass of each.
flow.say: Choose what to pack for the Moon, and then for Mars. The tent and water must go in. Add up the masses. Stay under the limit.
flow.kid: Pack for the Moon. Add the masses. Then pack for Mars.
flow.parent: Many packs work. A Moon pack could hold the tent, water, sleeping bag, food, camera, tools, first aid kit, rope and ladder. That is 27 kilograms. On Mars, only the tent, water, food, sleeping bag and first aid kit fit, which is 12 kilograms.

check.q: Which pack gets heavier for the same 50 newtons: on the Moon or on Earth?
options: The Moon pack carries more mass
The Earth pack carries more mass
check.why: On the Moon each kilogram weighs only 1.6 newtons, so 50 newtons holds about 31 kilograms. On Earth each kilogram weighs about 10 newtons, so 50 newtons holds about 5 kilograms. The pack with more mass is the Moon pack.

flow.context: This step of the 50-Newton Pack is the packing. Here you choose items for two worlds.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what will be hard about turning round with a 31 kilogram pack on the Moon. 2. Ask them to use the Hit the Bottles activity as evidence. 3. Write the answer. 4. Choose a world and do your own pack.
flow.say: Your Moon pack feels as light as 5 kilograms when you hold it still. But when you turn round, does it feel light? Think of the full bottle that was hard to move sideways.
flow.kid: Your pack feels light when still. Is it easy to turn round with? Why?

ask.q: Is a 31 kilogram pack easy to turn round with on the Moon?
good: No, it still has 31 kilograms of mass, so it is hard to start and stop turning.
Mass is the same on every world.

flow.parent: The pack weighs only 50 newtons but has the mass of a 31 kilogram bag. Mass decides how hard it is to start moving or turn. Astronauts on the Moon found it easy to carry heavy things but hard to stop or turn them quickly.
flow.context: This is the last step of the 50-Newton Pack. Here you think about what mass does when you move.

worksheets.title: Mass, weight and the normal force (core)

items.p: Which of these is measured in newtons?
opts: The amount of matter in a mango
items.why: Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons. Mass is the amount of matter, and it is measured in kilograms and grams.

items.p: True or false: a mango has less mass on the Moon than on the Earth.
items.why: False. A mango has the same amount of matter on every world, so its mass does not change. Its weight is about six times smaller on the Moon.

items.p: A bag with a mass of 6 kilograms weighs about ____ newtons on the Earth.
items.why: Each kilogram weighs about 10 newtons on the Earth, for quick sums. So 6 times 10 is 60 newtons.

items.p: A girl has a mass of 40 kilograms. Each kilogram weighs 3.7 newtons on Mars. What does she weigh there, in newtons?
items.why: Multiply the mass by the strength of gravity. 40 times 3.7 is 148. She weighs 148 newtons on Mars, and her mass is still 40 kilograms.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the amount of matter in a thing
the pull of gravity on a thing
the push of a surface on a thing pressing it
a push or pull put on a thing by touching it
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each one.

items.p: Sort these forces by whether the things must touch.
items: the Earth's pull on a falling mango
the push of a table on a book
a magnet's pull on a pin
items.why: A hand, a table and a rope act only where they touch. Gravity and a magnet act across a gap.

items.p: A book rests on a level table and does not move. Which force stops it falling through the table?
opts: The normal force of the table
An applied force from the book
items.why: The table is squashed a tiny amount by the book, and it pushes back up. That push is the normal force. Gravity is what pulls the book down.

items.p: A book rests on a level table. Show the forces on the book.
items.obj: a book resting on a level table
items.why: Gravity pulls the book down. The table pushes it up just as hard, so the book stays still. Nobody is pushing it, and nothing is making it slide.

items.p: Draw a steel tumbler standing on a shelf. Add two arrows and label them.
items.a: A tumbler drawn as a box, with an arrow down labelled gravity and an arrow up labelled normal force, both the same length.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the gravity arrow down and the normal force arrow up, starting where the shelf touches the tumbler. The two arrows are the same length, because the tumbler is still.
items.art: A blank shelf with a steel tumbler on it and room for two arrows.

items.p: Explain why the dough at the bottom of a pile of books is squashed more than the dough at the top.
items.a: The bottom dough has the weight of all the books above it, and the top dough has only one. Each book rests on the one below, so the load grows towards the bottom. A greater push squashes the dough more.
items.why: A strong answer says that each level carries everything above it. It also says that more books mean a bigger push on the dough.

items.p: Which tool gives the same answer on the Earth and on the Moon?
items.why: A two-pan balance compares one mass with another, so the pull of the world cancels out. The other three measure a pull or a push, which is smaller on the Moon.

items.p: True or false: a table pushes up on a book because the table is squashed a tiny amount.
items.why: True. The book squashes the table by a tiny amount. The squashed particles push back, and that push holds the book up.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to find your weight on Mars.
a: Find the number for Mars, 3.7 newtons for each kilogram
items: Find the number for Mars, 3.7 newtons for each kilogram
items.why: First you need your mass, and then the number for the world. Then you multiply them. The answer is a force, so it is written in newtons.

items.p: Three of these are applied forces. Which one is not?
opts: A hand pressing a rolling pin
items.why: An applied force is a push or pull from a person, an animal or a machine that touches the thing. The Earth pulls a mango without touching it.

items.p: A girl stands on a bathroom scale on the floor. Label three forces on her, or on the scale.
a: The Earth's pull on the girl, down
The scale's push on the girl, up
The floor's push on the scale, up
items.why: The girl stays still, so the scale pushes up on her as hard as gravity pulls her down. The scale reads that push. The floor must push up on the scale with the girl's weight and the scale's own weight.
items.art: A girl standing on a bathroom scale on a floor, with three blank label lines.

worksheets.title: Weights on other worlds and force arrows (stretch)

items.p: A 2 kilogram pack is at Jupiter's cloud tops, where each kilogram weighs about 25 newtons. About what does it weigh?
items.why: Multiply the mass by the strength of gravity. 2 times 25 is 50 newtons. Choosing 25 forgets to multiply by the mass.

items.p: Saturn has 95 times the Earth's mass. Explain why its pull at the cloud tops is only a little bigger.
items.a: The pull depends on the mass of the world and on how far you are from its centre. Saturn's cloud tops are about 9.5 times as far from its centre as the Earth's surface is. The pull gets weaker by the distance multiplied by itself, so the distance counts twice. That cancels most of the extra mass.
items.why: A strong answer says that distance from the centre matters, and that it counts twice because the pull gets weaker by the distance multiplied by itself. It does not say that gas has no weight.

items.p: Jupiter has 318 times the Earth's mass and 11.2 times its width. About how many times as strong is its pull?
items.why: 11.2 times 11.2 is about 125.4. Then 318 divided by 125.4 is about 2.5. So the pull at Jupiter's cloud tops is about two and a half times the Earth's.

items.p: A string lifts a 1 kilogram packet until the scale under it reads 700 grams. Show the three forces on the packet.
items.obj: a packet on a kitchen scale, partly lifted by a string
items.why: Gravity pulls down with 10 newtons. The scale pushes up with 7 newtons and the string pulls up with 3. The two small up forces add up to the big down force, so the packet stays still.

items.p: A finger presses on a 1 kilogram packet, and the scale reads 1,500 grams. The finger presses with about ____ newtons.
items.why: The scale reads 15 newtons. The packet's weight is 10 newtons, so the finger adds 15 minus 10, which is 5 newtons.

items.p: True or false: without friction, a heavy cart needs less force to speed up on the Moon than on the Earth.
items.why: False. The force needed to speed a thing up depends on its mass, and mass is the same on the Moon. The cart is lighter, but it is not easier to start.

items.p: A packet weighs 10 newtons. A string pulls it up with 4 newtons. How hard does the table push up?
items.why: The string and the table together must hold up the 10 newton weight. The string gives 4, so the table gives 10 minus 4, which is 6 newtons.

items.p: Sort these into things that are the same on the Moon as on the Earth, and things that change.
items: how hard a trolley is to start moving
the reading of a spring scale
the reading of a two-pan balance
items.why: Mass, inertia and a balance's answer depend only on how much matter there is. Weight, a spring scale and the strength of gravity depend on the world.

items.p: Match each quantity to the unit it is measured in.
items.why: Weight is a force, so it uses newtons. The strength of gravity says how many newtons one kilogram weighs.

items.p: Three people talk about the word 'weight'.

views.says: Weight is what my scale shows. A packet that reads 1 kilogram weighs 1 kilogram.
Weight is the pull of gravity, in newtons. Kilograms measure mass.
I feel weightless, though gravity still pulls on me. So weight is what a surface pushes with.

items.ask: Whose use of the word do you prefer? Give two reasons from the unit. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and uses facts such as the Moon scale or the falling astronaut. It also says what another view gets right: the shopkeeper's scale really does show a push, and the astronaut really does feel no push.
items.why: All three describe something real. The facts agree. People only use the word 'weight' for different things.

items.p: Draw a boy hanging from a bar with his feet off the floor. Draw and label every force on him.
items.a: A boy drawn as a box, with an arrow down labelled gravity and an arrow up, the same length, labelled the pull of the bar on his hands. There is no arrow from the floor.
items.why: A strong drawing has two arrows of the same length, and none from the floor, because his feet do not touch it. The up arrow is from the bar, not a normal force from the floor.
items.art: A boy hanging from a horizontal bar with his feet above a floor, with room for arrows.

items.p: In Lift, Press and Tilt, the scale read less on a tilted board. Explain why, with words and an arrow.
items.a: The slope only stops the packet sinking into the board. The board pushes straight out from its surface, and that push is smaller than the weight. Something else, such as the tape in the experiment, has to hold the packet so that it does not slide down the slope.
items.why: A strong answer says that the normal force points straight out from the surface. On a slope it is smaller than the weight. It may draw a leaning arrow.

items.p: Which of these worlds gives the weakest pull at its surface?
items.why: The Moon's number is about 1.6 newtons for each kilogram. Mars and Mercury have 3.7, and Venus has 8.9.

items.p: Put these in order of how much a 10 kilogram bag weighs, from the smallest to the biggest.
items.why: The numbers are 1.6, 3.7, 9.8 and about 25 newtons for each kilogram. A bigger number means a bigger weight for the same mass.

items.p: Three of these push with a normal force. Which one does not?
opts: A wall against a leaning hand
A chair under a sitting person
The Earth pulling a falling ball
items.why: A floor, a wall and a chair are surfaces that touch the thing and push straight out from themselves. The Earth's pull on a ball is gravity, and it needs no touching.

worksheets.title: Reasoning with forces on worlds and pillars (challenge)

items.p: In many buildings the pillars on the ground floor are thicker than the pillars near the top. Explain why.
items.a: Each pillar holds up everything above it. A ground-floor pillar carries every floor above, and a top-floor pillar carries only the roof. So the lower pillars carry more load and need to be stronger.
items.why: A strong answer says that loads are passed down and add up, so the lowest pillars carry the most.

items.p: A world has 2 times the Earth's mass and 1.25 times its width. About how many times as strong is its pull?
items.why: 1.25 times 1.25 is 1.5625. Then 2 divided by 1.5625 is about 1.3. So the pull is about 1.3 times the Earth's.

items.p: Mars has about twice the mass of Mercury, and both pull with 3.7 newtons for each kilogram. What explains this?
opts: Mars is wider, so its surface is further from its centre
Mercury is closer to the Sun
Weight does not depend on mass
items.why: Mars has more mass, which pulls harder. But its surface is further from its centre, which pulls less. Here the two effects cancel almost exactly.

items.p: Three people talk about gravity.

views.says: I treat gravity as a force. My sums give the right loads on every bridge.
Gravity is the bending of space and time. Falling things follow the bend, and nothing pulls them.
To land on the Moon, I use Newton's force. The difference from Einstein's sums is far too small to matter.

items.ask: Which view would you use to design a bridge, and which to explain why things fall alike? Give a reason for each. Then say what another view gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the force view for bridges and everyday sums, because it is simple and accurate there. It may use the bending view to explain why every thing falls alike. It says that the views agree where they overlap.
items.why: Each view works in its own place. Einstein's view explains more, and Newton's view is easier to use.

items.p: A person would weigh 2.5 times as much at Jupiter's cloud tops. Why could a scale there not show this?
items.a: A scale shows the push between a person and a surface. Jupiter has no solid surface, so the person keeps sinking and nothing pushes back. There would be weight, but no normal force for the scale to read.
items.why: A strong answer says that a scale measures a push from a surface, and that there is no surface to push back.

items.p: True or false: the ground can push up on a runner's foot with 2 to 3 times her weight.
items.why: True. The foot pushes down hard, so the ground pushes up with more than the runner's weight. That bigger push stops her falling and makes her move.

items.p: Three of these have no normal force acting on them. Which one has a normal force?
opts: A ball at the top of a throw
An astronaut floating in the station
A girl floating in a pool, with her feet off the floor
items.why: The ball, the astronaut and the girl touch no solid surface that pushes on them. The book touches the shelf, which pushes up on it.

items.p: Sort these into things with balanced forces and things with unbalanced forces.
items: a bag held still in a hand
a stone just after it is dropped
a book resting on a table
a ball at the top of a throw
a lift speeding up on its way up
a car at a steady speed on a straight, level road
items.why: Balanced forces cancel, so the thing stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed. Unbalanced forces make a thing speed up, slow down or turn.

items.p: A tomato with a mass of 250 grams weighs about ____ newtons on the Earth.
items.why: 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. So 250 grams weighs about 2.5 newtons.

items.p: Match each situation to what the support does.
pairs: A book is pressed down by a finger
The table pushes more than the book's weight
A packet is lifted a little by a string
The scale pushes less than the packet's weight
A girl hangs from a bar
The floor does not push on her at all
One book lies alone on a level table
The table pushes as hard as the book's weight
items.why: A surface pushes only as hard as it needs to, to stop the thing sinking into it. Other forces on the thing change how hard that is.

items.p: Draw the forces on the middle book of a pile of three equal books. Give each arrow a length.
items.a: A box for the middle book, with an arrow down for gravity of 1 unit, an arrow down for the top book's push of 1 unit, and an arrow up for the bottom book's push of 2 units.
items.why: A strong drawing has two down arrows and one up arrow. The up arrow is as long as the two down arrows together, because the book is still.
items.art: A pile of three books, with the middle book outlined and room for arrows.

items.p: The Earth pulls an apple with a force of 1 newton. How hard does the apple pull the Earth?
items.why: Forces come in pairs. The apple pulls the Earth with the same force of 1 newton. The Earth is so massive that this pull moves it by too little to measure.

items.p: Many people think the normal force always equals the weight. Describe a home test that shows this is wrong.
items.a: Put a packet on a kitchen scale and press down on it with a finger. The scale reads more than the packet's weight, so the table's push is bigger than the weight. Lifting the packet with a string makes the reading smaller.
items.why: A strong answer names a test with a scale, a finger or a string, and says what the reading does. It says why that shows the normal force can change.

items.p: Put these in order of how hard the floor pushes on a girl, from the smallest to the biggest.
a: She hangs from a bar with her feet off the floor
She stands on a board tilted up at one end
She stands still on a level floor
She lands hard from a jump
items: She lands hard from a jump
She stands still on a level floor
She stands on a board tilted up at one end
She hangs from a bar with her feet off the floor
items.why: Hanging gives a push of zero. A tilted board gives less than her weight. A level floor gives exactly her weight. A hard landing gives more than her weight.

items.p: A pillar holds up 60 square metres of floor, each with a mass of 1,000 kilograms. Find the load in newtons.
items.why: 60 times 1,000 is 60,000 kilograms. Each kilogram weighs about 10 newtons, so 60,000 times 10 is 600,000 newtons.

quiz.p: Which of these is the same on every world?
opts: The reading of a spring scale
The pull of gravity on you
quiz.why: Mass is the amount of matter in you, and you take it with you to every world. The other three change with the strength of gravity.

quiz.p: A bag has a mass of 4 kilograms. About what does it weigh on the Earth?
quiz.why: Each kilogram weighs about 10 newtons on the Earth. So 4 kilograms weigh about 40 newtons.

quiz.p: A dog has a mass of 12 kilograms. About what does she weigh on the Moon, where each kilogram weighs 1.6 newtons?
quiz.why: Multiply the mass by the strength of gravity. 12 times 1.6 is 19.2 newtons. Choosing 120 uses the Earth's number instead of the Moon's.

quiz.p: Why is the pull at Saturn's cloud tops only a little more than the Earth's?
opts: Its cloud tops are far from its centre
quiz.why: Saturn has 95 times the Earth's mass, which alone would give a much bigger pull. But its cloud tops are about 9.5 times as far from its centre. The pull gets weaker by the distance multiplied by itself, which is about 9.5 times 9.5, or 90. That cancels most of the extra mass.

opts: The push of a surface on a thing pressing on it
The pull of gravity on a thing
The force that slows a sliding thing
quiz.why: The normal force is the push of a surface on a thing that presses on it. It points straight out from the surface. Gravity is a different force, and friction slows sliding.

quiz.p: A packet rests on a kitchen scale. A string lifts it so the scale reads less. What happens to the packet's weight?
quiz.why: Gravity pulls the packet just as hard as before. The reading is smaller because the string carries part of the weight, so the scale pushes less.

quiz.p: Which of these is an applied force?
quiz.why: An applied force is a push or pull put on a thing by touching it. A hand on a swing does this. The Earth and a magnet act across a gap.

quiz.p: A ball leaves your hand and flies up. Which of these is true?
opts: The push of your hand fades away slowly
The push of your hand ended when the ball left it
The ball carries the same push as before
The hand pulls the ball back
quiz.why: An applied force is a contact force, so it ends when the touching ends. After that, only gravity and the air act on the ball.

quiz.p: A book rests on a table. How long is the normal force arrow, compared with the gravity arrow?
quiz.why: The book is still, so the forces on it are balanced. The table pushes up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down.

quiz.p: A 5 newton book is pressed down with 3 newtons. How long is the table's arrow, at 1 centimetre for each newton?
quiz.why: The table must push up against the weight and the press together. 5 plus 3 is 8 newtons, so the arrow is 8 centimetres.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not know?
opts: Why the mass that pulls is the same as the mass that resists
quiz.why: Every test finds that a thing's mass sets its weight and how hard it is to speed up. The two always match. Nobody has a final reason why.

quiz.p: Why is the bottom storey of a tall building built strongest?
opts: It carries the weight of every floor above it
It is heavier than the other floors
It is nearest to the Sun
quiz.why: Each storey holds up everything above it, so the load grows towards the bottom.

applications: Engineers add up the load on every pillar, beam and foundation of a building, from the roof down to the ground. The lowest parts carry the most.
Bathroom scales, kitchen scales and baby scales measure the push between a thing and the scale, and show it as a mass. They are set for the strength of gravity on Earth.

Space agencies, such as ISRO, work out the weight of a rover or lander on the Moon and Mars from its mass. To test a machine on Earth, they can use cables or balloons that take some of its weight away.
Lorries, buses and trains are weighed on weighbridges and the load is limited, so that roads and bridges are not overloaded.
A lift has a limit in kilograms. When it starts to rise, its floor and cable must push and pull harder than the weight.
Athletes and dancers use the push of the ground. A jumper presses down on the ground and is pushed up with more than her weight.
Springboards, cots, mattresses and shoe soles are made soft so that they are squashed more and push back gently. This spreads the push and protects the body.
Geologists and surveyors measure small changes in the strength of gravity to find heavy rock or empty caves underground.

open_questions.q: Why is the mass that decides a thing's weight exactly the mass that makes it hard to move?
open_questions.why_open: Every test finds that the two match, to about one part in a thousand million million. Einstein's theory builds the match in, but nobody knows why nature is made that way.

open_questions.q: Why do the smallest particles have the masses they do?
open_questions.why_open: The Higgs field gives some particles their mass, and it was found in 2012. But nobody knows why each particle's mass is the number it is. Most of the mass of a proton also comes from the energy of the forces inside it.

open_questions.q: Is gravity carried by tiny particles, as the other forces are?
open_questions.why_open: Such a particle is called a graviton. Nobody has found one. Nobody has yet joined the physics of gravity with the physics of the very small.

open_questions.q: What is the mass we cannot see in galaxies, which scientists call dark matter?
open_questions.why_open: Stars at the edges of galaxies move as if there were much more mass than we can see. Nobody has found out what this mass is made of.

The Juno spacecraft measured Jupiter's gravity and found that the middle is probably not a small solid core. It may be a large, fuzzy region of rock and ice mixed into hydrogen. Scientists are still working on it.

ask_kids: Which things in this room are being pushed up by something right now? What is pushing them?
When you sit down, what is pushing on you? How hard is it pushing?
If you carried this bag to the Moon, would it be easier to lift? Would it be easier to throw hard?
Is it harder to lift a full bucket or to swing it round on a rope? Why?
What is at the bottom of the pile of clothes, books or plates, and how much weight is it holding?
The stairs hold you up. What holds up the stairs?
Which of your friends or family members works like the bottom book in a pile?
Why do we stand on the ground and not sink into it?

jokes.j: Why was the book at the bottom of the pile so calm?
jokes.a: It was used to being under pressure.

jokes.j: What did the table say to the book?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I've got your back. And your front, and your sides.

jokes.j: Why did the bathroom scale love the Moon?
What did the astronaut say about Jupiter?
jokes.a: There is no floor, but at least there is no cleaning.

jokes.j: What is a pillar's favourite sport?
jokes.a: Weightlifting, because it never gets tired.

jokes.j: Why was the force diagram so calm?
How does a rover start on the Moon?
jokes.a: Slowly, so that its wheels get a grip.

jokes.j: What did the mass say to the weight?
jokes.a: You change from world to world, but I will always be me.

jokes.j: Why did the ball have no normal force at the top of its throw?
jokes.a: It was not in touch with anyone.

maths.problem: A packet reads 1,240 grams on a kitchen scale. What is its weight in newtons? Round to one decimal place.
maths.explain: 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. So divide 1,240 by 100, which is 12.4. The packet weighs about 12.4 newtons.
maths.context: This is about Lift, Press and Tilt. A kitchen scale reads grams, and you turn the reading into newtons to draw the forces.
maths.why_maths: A scale reads in grams, but a force is measured in newtons. Dividing by 100 turns one into the other.

maths.problem: The Moon rover has a mass of 26 kilograms. Each kilogram weighs 9.8 newtons on the Earth and 1.62 newtons on the Moon. How many times smaller is its weight on the Moon?
maths.explain: On the Earth, 26 times 9.8 is 254.8 newtons. On the Moon, 26 times 1.62 is 42.12 newtons. 254.8 divided by 42.12 is about 6. The rover weighs about 6 times less.
maths.context: This is about the story The Slow Start. A rover goes from the Earth to the Moon, and its weight changes but its mass does not.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the mass by two different numbers shows how much the weight changes, while the mass stays 26 kilograms.

maths.problem: In a made-up Dough Stack result, the dough under 1 book was 26 millimetres wide, and under 8 books it was 47. The load grew 8 times. How many times wider was the dough? What does that say?
maths.answer: About 1.8 times wider. The width did not grow 8 times.
maths.explain: 47 divided by 26 is about 1.8. The load grew 8 times, but the width grew only 1.8 times. So the width is not in proportion to the load. A wider ball also has more dough to push back, so it can carry more load without spreading as fast.
maths.context: This is about the Dough Stack. The balls under more books were squashed wider.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how many times each number grows shows whether two things change in proportion, or in a different way.

maths.problem: In the Spreading Square, the sides of the lit square were 6, 12 and 18 centimetres. Work out the area of each square. How many times bigger is each area than the first?
maths.answer: 36, 144 and 324 square centimetres. So the areas are 1, 4 and 9 times the first.
maths.explain: The area of a square is the side times itself. 6 times 6 is 36. 12 times 12 is 144. 18 times 18 is 324. 144 divided by 36 is 4, and 324 divided by 36 is 9.
maths.context: This is about the Spreading Square. A light shines through a square hole onto a screen at three distances.
maths.why_maths: The area grows with the side times itself. Working it out shows that twice the distance gives four times the area.

maths.problem: A planet has the same mass as the Earth but is 3 times as wide. By what number must the pull be divided? What if it were 5 times as wide?
maths.answer: By 9 for 3 times as wide, and by 25 for 5 times as wide.
maths.explain: The pull is divided by the width times the width. 3 times 3 is 9. 5 times 5 is 25. So a planet 5 times as wide, with the same mass, would pull 25 times less.
maths.context: This is about Pull Detective. The strength of gravity at a world's surface depends on its mass and its width.
maths.why_maths: Squares and square numbers show how fast the pull falls as a world gets wider.

maths.problem: A pack may weigh at most 50 newtons. On Mars each kilogram weighs 3.7 newtons. What is the biggest whole number of kilograms you can carry?
maths.explain: 50 divided by 3.7 is about 13.5. You cannot carry half a kilogram over the limit, so round down to 13 kilograms. Check: 13 times 3.7 is 48.1 newtons, which is under 50.
maths.context: This is about the 50-Newton Pack. You work out how much mass a limit of 50 newtons holds on another world.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a weight limit by the strength of gravity gives the biggest mass. Rounding down keeps the pack under the limit.

maths.problem: A pillar holds up 18 square metres of floor on each of 5 floors. Each square metre of one floor has a mass of about 1,000 kilograms. What is the weight above the pillar, in newtons?
maths.explain: 18 times 5 is 90 square metres. 90 times 1,000 is 90,000 kilograms. 90,000 times 10 is 900,000 newtons.
maths.context: This is about the Load on the Pillar. A ground-floor pillar holds up every floor above it.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the area, the number of floors and the mass for each square metre gives a rough size for the load. It shows why one pillar needs to be so strong.

maths.problem: A packet marked 1 kilogram reads 1,012 grams on a kitchen scale. By what percentage is the reading bigger than the mark? What could cause the difference?
maths.answer: About 1.2 per cent. The packet may hold a little extra, or the scale may be a little off.
maths.explain: The reading is 12 grams over 1,000 grams. 12 divided by 1,000 is 0.012, which is 1.2 per cent. Packs are often filled a little over, and a scale can have a small error. Checking the scale with a known mass tells you which.
maths.context: This is about Lift, Press and Tilt. The packet is never exactly 1 kilogram, so every reading is a little different.
maths.why_maths: A percentage shows how big a difference is compared with the whole, so a small error can be judged fairly.

warmup.q: Which is measured in newtons: mass or weight?
warmup.a: Weight. Mass is measured in kilograms.

warmup.q: Does your mass change on the Moon?
warmup.a: No. Your mass is the same on every world. Your weight is about six times smaller.
The push of a surface on a thing that presses on it, straight out from the surface.

warmup.q: A book rests on a table. How big is the table's push?
warmup.a: As big as the book's weight, so the book stays still.
A push or a pull that a person, an animal or a machine puts on a thing by touching it.

warmup.q: Which tool shows the same answer on the Moon: a balance or a spring scale?
warmup.a: A balance, because it compares two masses.

warmup.q: In a pile of books, which level carries the most?

warmup.q: Why can't you stand on Jupiter?
warmup.a: It has no solid surface to push back. You would keep sinking.

quiz: A bathroom scale marked in kilograms would show about one sixth as much on the Moon.
It measures a push, and the Moon pulls about six times less.
A thing weighs less on the Moon because it has less mass there.
Its mass is the same. The Moon pulls less, so its weight is smaller.
A table pushes up on a book because it is squashed a tiny amount.
The squashed particles of the table push back on the book.
The normal force on a thing always equals its weight.
Pressing on the thing makes the push bigger. Lifting it with a string makes it smaller.
Jupiter has a solid surface to stand on.
Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium gas, and it gets thicker with depth.
The Earth pulls you, and you pull the Earth just as hard.
Forces come in pairs. The Earth is so massive that your pull moves it by far too little to notice.
The bottom book in a pile carries the weight of every book above it.
Each book rests on the one below, so the load adds up towards the bottom.
A thrown ball carries the push of the hand along with it.
The hand's push ends when the touching ends. The ball keeps moving by itself.
With no friction, a heavy trolley is as hard to start moving on the Moon as on the Earth.
How hard a thing is to start moving depends on its mass, and mass does not change.
Saturn pulls much harder at its cloud tops than the Earth does at its surface.
Saturn is so wide that the pull at its cloud tops is only a little stronger than the Earth's.
odd: Weight, gravity and the normal force are all forces, but mass is an amount of matter.
Kilograms, grams and tonnes are units of mass, but the newton is a unit of force.
A hand, a bullock and a crane touch the thing, but gravity acts across a gap.
The Moon, Mars and Mercury all weigh you less than the Earth does. Jupiter weighs you more.
A table, a floor and a chair push up with a normal force. A falling mango touches nothing.
