how_we_found_out.context: How do we know what a kilogram is? This card tells how one lump of metal defined it for 130 years. It also tells which idea about the lump turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1889, a small cylinder of platinum and iridium was chosen to be the kilogram. It is about as tall and as wide as a plum, and it had been made in 1879. It is kept in a locked vault near Paris, and people call it Le Grand K. Copies were made and sent to many countries. India's copy is kept at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi. Everyone believed that the master lump never changed. A kilogram was the mass of that lump, so it could not be wrong. From 1988 to 1992, and again in 2014, scientists compared the master with its copies. The copies had drifted away from it by about 50 micrograms in a hundred years. That is about the mass of a speck of fine dust. No one could say which lump had changed, because each was only measured against the others. So on 20 May 2019, the kilogram was defined using a fixed number from nature, called the Planck constant. The new method uses a Kibble balance, invented by Bryan Kibble in 1975. It balances the weight of a mass against an electric force. Because weight depends on gravity, the strength of gravity at its place must be measured very exactly.
how_we_found_out.who: The scientists of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures near Paris, who compared the lumps, and Bryan Kibble, who invented the balance
how_we_found_out.when: The lump was chosen in 1889. It was compared with its copies from 1988 to 1992 and in 2014. The kilogram was redefined on 20 May 2019.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a master lump of metal never changes, and so can define the kilogram for ever. The comparisons showed the copies and the master drifting apart by about 50 micrograms in a hundred years.
how_we_found_out.art: A small shining metal cylinder under two glass bell jars on a stand in a vault, with a scientist in a white coat looking at it through a magnifying glass.

roots.context: In this unit you squashed dough under a pile of books and saw the load grow towards the bottom. Here we ask what that says about how things stay up, and about us.

deep_truth.truth: In the Dough Stack, the dough under eight books was squashed far wider than the dough under one book. Every book rests on the one below, so each level carries everything above it. The bottom book is held up by the table, the table by the floor, and the floor by the Earth. So no book in a pile holds itself up.
deep_truth.habit: We say a table stands or a book sits, as if each held itself up. Everything that stays up is held by something else, and that is held by something else again.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dough Stack, the bottom ball carried the weight of all eight books and the top ball carried one. In Lift, Press and Tilt, the scale pushed up exactly as hard as the packet and the finger pressed on it. In the Load on the Pillar, a ground-floor pillar carried every floor above it.

three.who_am_i: You stand because the floor pushes up on you, and the floor is held up by the building and the ground. The whole Earth under you holds you up.
three.what_is_life: Every animal that stands, sits or walks is held up by the ground. A tree stands because her roots and trunk push on the ground, and the ground pushes back.
three.what_is_this_world: In a pile of books, a building or a planet, each part rests on another. The weight of everything above is passed down, and in the end the Earth holds it.

roots.thread: A book, a table, a floor, a pillar and the ground look like separate things. In the Dough Stack and the Load on the Pillar, they work as one chain. Each link pushes up on the link above it with a force equal to the weight of everything above. At the bottom is the Earth, which pulls the whole pile down and also holds it up. Many sages taught that nothing stands alone. A pile of books is a case where we can see this clearly, and we can draw it with arrows.

teachings.source: Atharva Veda 12.1.12 (the hymn to the Earth)
teachings.teaching: The Earth is my mother, and I am her child.
teachings.link: The verse speaks of the Earth as the one who holds us. In this unit, the Earth is the last link in every chain that holds something up. The verse is a statement of faith and care, and the unit does not test it.

teachings.teaching: A person uses only the small patch of ground under her feet. But if the earth around her were dug away down to the Yellow Springs, that small patch would be no use to her.
teachings.link: A pillar or a foot seems to need only the ground it touches. But the ground there is held up by all the ground round it. The passage says this as a lesson about usefulness, not about weight.

science.text: A surface pushes back on anything that presses on it, because the atoms of the two touching things repel each other. This push is the normal force.
Nobody knows why the mass that sets a thing's weight is exactly the mass that makes it hard to move.

other_view.view: Many physicists say that 'being held up by something' is only our way of adding up the forces between atoms. In their view there is no chain of holders, only a very large number of pushes between neighbouring atoms.

practice.title: Feel your whole weight go down
practice.say: Stand still in bare feet. Close your eyes. Feel the soles of your feet pressing on the floor. The floor pushes back with exactly your weight. Think of the floor resting on walls or pillars, and those on the ground. Take five slow breaths, and feel that whole chain holding you. Then open your eyes.
practice.kid: Stand in bare feet. Close your eyes. Feel your feet on the floor. The floor pushes up on you. The floor rests on the ground. Take five slow breaths. Open your eyes.

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. The Dough Stack (core) needs eight books of about the same size and stiff atta dough. How wide the balls spread depends on the stiffness and the weight of the books, so the trial step tells you to make the dough stiffer or softer first. Dough keeps flowing slowly, so the 5 minutes matter. The widths will not go up in exact steps. Lift, Press and Tilt (core) needs a kitchen scale in grams and a 1 kilogram packet. Some scales are a little off when tilted, so the readings on the board may differ from the expected 980, 940 and 870 grams by a few percent. The scale must be zeroed while tilted and empty. A grown-up should stand by for the tilt part. The Spreading Square needs a dark room and a phone torch, which is nearly a point of light. A torch with a mirror behind the bulb gives a beam that does not spread in the same way. The edges of the lit square are fuzzy, so the sides will be about 6, 12 and 18 centimetres, give or take a centimetre. It is a model of how a pull spreads out, and not a measurement of gravity. Hit the Bottles needs a stick across two heavy chairs and a grown-up to check it. The full bottle may swing only 1 or 2 centimetres, so a phone film helps. The other activities need only paper, a calculator, books and the kitchen scale. Be the Table needs a grown-up to press on the books. The Load on the Pillar needs a building with at least three floors and a grown-up. The Three-Storey Paper Tower depends on how well the tubes are rolled and taped. The first step tests one tube, so the number of loads can be changed. The 50-Newton Pack is a paper and calculator challenge, and the bag of 5 bottles is only to feel the load. No part needs a garden or an animal. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: the strengths of gravity and masses (NASA fact sheets), the kilogram story (BIPM, NIST, CSIR-NPL), the Pragyan figures, the Galileo probe, the Apollo 15 drop and the two verses. Softened: the astronaut's mass is now 'more than 150 kilograms'; the cable test is now 'cables or balloons'; the Apollo rocks line no longer claims they were weighed on both worlds; the giant-planet numbers are marked as worked out from NASA's masses and widths. Still a rough rule of thumb: 1,000 kilograms for each square metre of floor. The story's wheel grip and cable test is imagined.
